title: Midnight
logline: Christmas week on Glenwood Avenue: a game on two televisions, a brother across a bolted table, a guest who isn’t company anymore — and a phone that won’t stay in the basket.

previously.text: In a car with no future, at one in the morning: “Go home. Text me from the snow globe. When you get back, we’re dating. Officially.” … “I’ll make it a whole thing.”
Father Osei, behind the screen: “You are not avoiding the occasion, my friend. You are scheduling it.”

Laney, with her hand on your chain: “Whatever this is, fireman, you are fixin’ to fix it. Or I will end you.” Theo, from the car: “Have a good Christmas, Costigan. All of it. And answer your phone in Ohio.”
On the Lighthouse porch: “Something’s hurting you… Bad. I can see that much from here.”
On the Lagoon bench: “Call me Christmas Eve. I’ll be on the levee. I’ll hold the phone up so you can hear it burn.”
In Denver the phone came back on. *Fourteen and oh tonight. It’s ordained. Merry Christmas, Youngstown. —L.*

s01.slug: SATURDAY · 4:55 PM · PITTSBURGH INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT → ROUTE 60 NORTH
body: Western Pennsylvania comes up under the cloud floor all at once, and it’s white. The jet drops through the last of the gray with its wing light blinking — on, and the snow streams past it sideways, every flake lit; off, and there’s only the wing — and below it the ground is laid out in white squares stitched together with black lines of trees, a farm pond frozen flat, a county road drawn on it in headlights. After a December of fog and sixty degrees he had forgotten it could do this: just fall, all afternoon, for no reason but December. He keeps his forehead on the plastic until the runway comes up and takes the snow away under the wheels.
At the gate he holds the red key down, and walks up the jetway with the RAZR waking in his hand.
Every other step, through the pocket of the Carhartt, the corner of the tin finds his hip.
He reads the stack on the long escalator down to baggage claim, standing on one step with his hands full of phone while the snow goes past the tall glass wall beside him.

body: His father is at the bottom of the escalator. He has the Browns knit hat on with snow still caught in the weave — he walked over from short-term, then, rather than circle — and the thermos under one arm like a football, and he watches Jack come down without waving. He says, “Which one,” meaning the carousel, and walks him to it, and when the duffel comes around Frank has it off the belt and the strap settled on his own shoulder before Jack can get a hand to it. Then he hugs him, with the arm that’s free. One arm. The thermos between them; the wet wool of the hat against Jack’s ear.
“You eat?”
“On the plane.”
“That’s not eating.”
Somebody gave him that one in the kitchen this morning. As soon as it’s out, Frank looks off down the belt.

They go out across the walkway to short-term with the snow blowing in under the roof of it, Frank a half step ahead with the duffel. He won’t give it back. The Silverado is on the second level with two inches on the hood. Frank starts it, and unscrews the thermos and pours the lid full and holds it out — coffee, Ma’s, from the house, still hot after two and a half hours — and while Jack drinks it he gets the scraper out from behind the seat and clears the windshield in long strokes with the engine running. The duffel rides in the middle of the bench seat with the lap belt across it, because Frank belts it.

Route 60 north is two black ruts in the slush and the taillights of a salt truck. The wipers go. The defrost is on high and KDKA is on low: a man counting accidents on the Parkway, the Steelers tomorrow against Green Bay, a woman who wants to sell them gutters. Somewhere past Moon Township Frank says, “Your sister’s been on that computer in the basement every night since Thanksgiving. Says it’s for school.”
“It’s for school.”
“Uh huh.” The wipers. “Tests go alright?”
“Good. I find out Monday.”
“Good.” A semi goes by on the left and buries them in slush, and the wipers fight their way out of it. “Hall’s got a list up.”
“For what?”
“The small car.” The wipers go across and back. “Spring.” Across and back. “Maybe.”
That’s the news. Beaver County goes by unseen, the snow coming at the glass out of the black, thrown. After a mile of wipers:
“Your mother says there’s a girl.”

response: Frank drives a mile. A plow passes going the other way with its orange light turning on the snow, and the truck rocks in its wake.
“Not the Saints one.”
“No.”
Another mile.
“Okay.”

Past New Castle the snow thins to a few flakes swimming in the high beams. The sign for Ohio comes up white with a ridge of snow along its top edge, and goes by. Down along the river below the road, where the Valley opens out in the dark, what’s left of the mills stands in the snow: a run of sheds with the roofing long gone and a furnace frame beside them, the steel ribs of it in rows against the sky, and snow laid along every crosspiece, white lines drawn on black.
Frank, to the windshield: “Your mother says it ain’t.”
The wipers go across and back, and the salt truck ahead of them throws a spray of it against the glass.
“God help you,” his father says, and that’s all he says till Ohio.

body: Frank has strung blue lights around the bathtub Madonna in the side yard, three times around the tub and once over the top, and they’ve got snow on them now, and so has she: a little on each shoulder, a little in each of her two open hands. Two doors up, the neighbors’ inflatable has been changed over to a Santa, and the Santa is lying face-down in the yard. In the front window the tree is up with every ornament Jack made at St. Brigid’s in second grade still on it, the paper-plate angel with his school picture for a face, and along the mantel the stockings hang in their row with the names on the cuffs in Ma’s glitter glue: FRANK, MARIA, DANNY, JACK, GINA, ROSIE, NONNA.

Gina has the storm door open while he’s still on the steps. She hugs him like a normal person, arms around his neck, her cheek against the snow on the Carhartt, and says into his collar, low, “Did she send you anything.”
“*Just asking.*” She lets go and puts both hands in the front pocket of her sweatshirt, where they can’t do anything.

Rosie is behind her in pajamas with a drawing held up in both hands at the height of his face: Jack, very tall, beside a crab the size of a dog and a Christmas tree with a star bigger than either of them. “That’s you,” she says. “That’s a crab.” And Ma, from the kitchen doorway with a dish towel over her shoulder: “Did you eat? You didn’t eat. I can hear it.” She gets to him past both girls and takes his face in her two hands, wet dish towel and all, and kisses him on the side of the head. “You smell like an airplane.” Behind him Frank comes up the steps with the duffel, stamps the snow off on the mat, and sets it down by the radiator without a word.

On the mantel, over the stockings, the Christmas cards stand open in a row, and at the front of the row, where you’d see it first from the door, is one on stationery with cows on it, and Ma has stood it there and says nothing about it. Jack knows the cows from the mat, with one boot off. Later, up close, it says *To the Costigans* in round blue ballpoint, and *Praying for Mrs. Rinaldi’s hand*.
Nonna is in her chair by the front window with the San Giovanni rosary in her left hand, and on the right, where the cast was, a beige splint with Velcro straps.
“Giacomino.”

He kneels on the rug by the chair so she won’t have to look up, and she takes his face in her left hand and turns it to the lamp to see what California has done to it. “Nonna. There’s a lady in New Orleans who lights a candle for you every Sunday. Mémère. She told me to tell you she’s still lighting the whole name.”
Nonna’s chin comes up off her chest. “Carmela Rinaldi,” she says, the way she says it to doctors. “*Tutto.*”

He tells her a priest in California turned around on his church steps toward Ohio and made a cross in the air for her, by name. “Carmela,” she agrees, pleased with him, like he’s finally got it right.

Rosie wants to know what’s in the duffel. He unbuckles the strap to get at the stuffed buffalo he bought her in the Denver airport, and Theo’s gray throw, rolled tight under the strap since the Delgado lobby, comes loose and unrolls across the rug to Nonna’s slippers. Rosie takes the buffalo and names it Denver on the spot. Nonna’s left hand goes down to the throw. She rubs a corner between her thumb and the side of her finger.
“*Questo è di qualcuno ricco.*”

It goes over her knees. “Is that the rich one’s?” Ma says from the doorway. “It was,” Jack says. By the time Ma has gone back to the stove it’s been tucked in at both sides, and Nonna has her hand flat on it.
Then Nonna looks past him at the front door. “*Viene Danny?*”
Ma, with the dish towel: “Not this year, Ma.”
Nonna nods at that, and moves a bead along, and then her eyes come up to Jack, black and perfectly clear, in front of Ma. “*E l’attrice?*”
“She means Gina’s show,” Ma says.
On the stairs Gina coughs on nothing, hard, and has to hold the banister.

response: “Più tardi,” she agrees, and pats his cheek with the good hand, satisfied. Five minutes later, with his coat off and Rosie on his knee explaining the buffalo to him, she asks again, as new: “*E l’attrice?*”

There’s a place.”
“Frank,” Maria says, from the stove.
“I know.”
She lifts the rosary at him like a fist, the crucifix swinging off the bottom of it. Gina goes up the rest of the stairs as fast as a person can go without running, and a door shuts.

s03.slug: SATURDAY · 8:20 PM · A BAR ON MARKET STREET
s03.music: The Pogues feat. Kirsty MacColl — “Fairytale of New York”
body: The place on Market Street has a Stroh’s sign in the window with the S burned out and no other name anybody uses. Inside: a long bar under a pressed-tin ceiling, Christmas lights stapled along the top of the backbar mirror, and a television over the register that gets NFL Network because the owner’s brother-in-law is a Cowboys fan and pays for it. A dozen men in work coats and Browns knits. Most of them say *Frankie* when the door lets him in. Frank takes the stool at the end, under the set, and the bartender comes down to him.
“Canada Dry,” Frank says. “In a glass.”

The bartender looks at him once and takes down a glass. Jack gets a Coke. On the set the Saints are lining up to receive in the Superdome under a noise that makes the speaker over the register buzz, and Frank, who has never cared what happens to New Orleans on a Saturday night, turns his stool to watch them. His son is watching.

At 8:22 the RAZR goes off in his coat. It’s Lena, and behind Lena it’s a room: a television turned up past what it’s for, a man yelling at it, a woman saying something low in French, the clunk of a vending machine.

“That’s Daddy,” she says, about the yelling. “In the Brees jersey. He wore it to the hospital; he’ll be buried in it. Mémère brought a Thermos *pour la mère* and she’s drinking it herself. Luc’s on his break, so there’s a policeman in the maternity ward eating Zapp’s. Beau’s in and out of that door like a cuckoo clock. Josie’s doing the play-by-play for the nurses’ station.” Her breath catches up with her. “You said the garage.”
“The garage doesn’t get NFL Network. Neither does the house. I’m in a bar with my father.”
“Your *father’s* in a bar?”
Jack turns on the stool, away from the end of the bar. “Drinking a ginger ale,” he says, lower.

On her end the room goes on — Tony telling the referees exactly what they are, a page for a doctor, the vending machine again — and under it her breath against the phone. “Tell him I said thank you for bringing you.”
Frank’s eyes don’t leave the set. “Tell her you’re welcome.”

So the game comes to him on two televisions. The one over the register runs a second or two ahead of the one bolted to the wall at Touro, and every play happens twice: once in the bar on Market Street, and once again a breath later in New Orleans, where Tony takes it worse. A Dallas run up the middle gets a groan from the Cowboys fan’s end of the bar and then, from the phone, a word Lena tells him her father is going to confess.
A man two stools down in a Local 1112 jacket leans back to look past Jack. “Who’s he on with, Frankie?”
“New Orleans,” Frank says.
“The whole city?”
“Most of it.”

Between plays she starts on Pius. “You saw. Your man made him venerable this morning, him and John Paul on the same piece of paper, and Daddy and Luc have been at it since the Rouses.” “Which side’s your father on?” “Whichever side Luc isn’t.” “And you?” “I’ll tell you when you’ve picked yours.” And Dallas is in the red zone, and Pius has to wait.

The first half belongs to Dallas. Lena takes every first down personally, on behalf of the waiting room and the city and, she says, the Holy See. At the half, in the middle of a sentence about the officiating, her LG dies. The last thing he hears before it goes is Josie, close to the phone, wanting it on the record that she called this in August.

The bar uses the half to stretch. Somebody feeds the jukebox, and the Pogues come on, the drunk man and the woman going at each other over the piano, and two old men at the far end who have known each other since Sheet & Tube sing the parts they know into each other’s faces, badly, with feeling. Frank drinks his ginger ale. Jack sits with the dead phone in his hand.
At two past ten it buzzes with a number he doesn’t know, and it’s her voice. “Remy’s,” she says. “Mine’s dead and his smells like a fraternity.”

The third quarter belongs to Dallas too. Somewhere in it she gets the 8-Ball out of her coat — he hears the slosh of the blue water, and the waiting room telling her to do it — and asks it, in front of everybody, whether the Saints are going to win this game. She reads him the window. “*Very doubtful.*” The waiting room groans at the news. “I’m going to throw it in the bayou.”

At a quarter past ten, Dallas driving again, a door bangs open on her end and the room goes up — a roar he takes for a touchdown until it keeps going past where a touchdown stops. Tony is shouting. Mémère is shouting in French. Somebody is crying in the high, helpless way that means good news, and then it’s Lena, crying and laughing and talking over her father: “She came, Jack. She came while they were undefeated. Beau doesn’t get a vote. It’s on the napkin. Luc *witnessed*.”
“What’s her name?”

“Lucille.” He hears her wipe her face on something, a sleeve. “For Grandmère. Odile in the middle, for Mémère, so nobody fights.” Over her shoulder, to someone: “I’m *telling* him.” And to him: “They’re letting us in two at a time and Mémère says she’s first, she says she’s earned it. Keep watching. Tell me everything.”
She’s gone. Jack puts the phone on the bar. “It’s a girl,” he says.
Frank watches Dallas line up for a field goal. “Healthy?”
“She says she’s got a lot of hair.”
Frank nods. He picks up the ginger ale and tips it at the television, at New Orleans, at whoever’s in charge down there, and drinks.

Brees comes back. A touchdown, and the men at the end of the bar, who have no business caring, make a noise anyway; another, and it’s seven, and three of them have turned into Saints fans for the night, and the brother-in-law has gone to stand by the pool table with his arms folded. The RAZR buzzes on the bar. Lena, from a hallway, with a cart going by — he can hear its wheels: “Tess asked me. To be godmother. With the epidural still in.”
“Yeah?”
“I said yes before she got to the *mother*.”
On the set the last drive ends. Dallas 24, New Orleans 17. The bar goes back to its drinks.
“She came in undefeated,” she says. “You watched the first one we lost. I’m not saying it’s your fault. I’m saying it’s a pattern. And don’t you say Detroit to me tonight.”

choices.text: “She came in undefeated. That’s the record that counts.”
response: “She came in undefeated,” Jack says. “That’s the record that counts.”

The line is quiet on her end, and then he hears Tony, in the waiting room, telling everybody what the Ohio boy said, and getting it wrong, and the waiting room agreeing with him anyway. “Daddy says you’re a theologian,” Lena says, when she can. “I told him you’re from Ohio. He said that’s worse.”

choices.text: “Thirteen and one. The Browns would kill a man for that.”
response: “Thirteen and one,” Jack says. “The Browns would kill a man for that.”
Frank, to the set: “We would.” And Lena laughs, with the crying still in it, and tells the waiting room, and the waiting room tells her the Browns are a tragedy, and she passes that on too.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let her have it.
response: He keeps the phone at his ear and lets her have it. The waiting room, Tony’s voice going hoarse, somebody’s rosary clicking against a chair. A commercial for trucks on the set over his head. The line stays open.
“You’re still there,” she says.
“I’m here.”

s03a.slug: SATURDAY · 11:40 PM · THE SILVERADO, MARKET STREET → GLENWOOD AVENUE
body: Market Street has been plowed once and salted twice, and the salt comes up gray in the headlights. The wipers knock the new snow off the glass. Lena is still on the line. She’s on the floor of Tess’s room now, she tells him, with her back against the heater under the window, and the baby is asleep, and Tess is asleep, and Beau is asleep in the chair with his mouth open, and she is staying on the phone until somebody in authority makes her stop. She keeps her voice down for all three of them.
“She has so much hair,” she says. “Jack. It’s *indecent*.”
“Whose side is it from?”
“Mémère says hers. Daddy says his. Daddy’s bald.” The heater ticks behind her. “Her bracelet goes around my thumb. I tried it.”
“Did they let you hold her?”
“Second. After Mémère.” Her voice goes down another notch. “She looked right at me. They can’t see yet, I know they can’t. She did it anyway.”

He doesn’t say anything to that, and she doesn’t ask him to. The truck goes down Market Street at thirty miles an hour with the two of them on it. What Mémère said to the night nurse in French, Lena won’t translate.
Somewhere at her end a door opens. A woman’s voice, low, about a blood pressure, and then nearer, amused: “That your boyfriend?”
“My friend in Ohio,” Lena says.
Frank keeps the truck in the plowed track. The salt goes by in the lights.
At the corner of Glenwood she lets him go. “I’m sending you her,” she says. “When the nurses are done with her. Don’t you dare show anybody who’ll say she looks like Tony.” And she hangs up.
Frank drives a block of Glenwood with the wipers going. “Her sister had a baby during the game?”
“Third quarter.”
The light at Midlothian is red over nothing. Frank sits it out anyway, both hands on the wheel, and when it goes green and they’re through it: “That’s a Catholic family.”

The wedding soup is still on low at twenty to one, the lid lifting and settling on the pot. Ma is up — not waiting up; she would want that understood — at the counter in her robe, writing a list on the back of an envelope. Through the doorway Nonna is awake in her chair with the lamp on, and Gina is at the kitchen table in a Cardinal Mooney sweatshirt that used to be Danny’s, eating soup out of a mug with a fork, for the meatballs.

He has been telling Ma about the game for ten minutes, because she asked: Lena’s sister in labor through three quarters, Lena’s father in a Brees jersey yelling at a television bolted to a hospital wall, Lena’s grandmother with a Thermos for the mother, Lena saying the baby came in undefeated so the father doesn’t get a vote. Across the table Gina has started putting up a finger every time he says the name, without looking up from the soup. She is on her second hand.
At 12:40 the RAZR buzzes in his coat on the back of the chair.

body: It comes the way they come on this phone: a gray square, a bar that fills from the left at its own pace, then a picture no bigger than his thumbnail, and he has to hold it under the stove-hood light to find the baby in it. A newborn in a striped hospital blanket, pink and white, asleep with her mouth open and one fist up by her ear like she’s got a question. Tess’s hand under her head. In the corner of the frame, out of focus, a loop of black beads that can only be Mémère’s.
“Is that the baby?” Ma is at his shoulder with the envelope. “Let me see the baby.”
From the front room: “*La bambina?*”
He’s in the inbox to get to it, and the baby is at the top of the list. Under her, down the little screen, the same small picture icon five more times.

Ma’s chin is at his ear. Rosie, woken by something, is on the stairs in her nightgown with her hair flat on one side. And Gina, who as far as he knows has never seen a picture on this phone, takes one look at her brother’s face and puts her fork down in the mug.

s04.slug: SUNDAY · 8:00 AM · ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE
body: All four candles on the Advent wreath are lit this morning, and they stand in a staircase, four Sundays of burning, the first one down to a stub and today’s new and tallest. Snow light comes in gray through the windows on the east side. They take their pew on the left, in the order they have always taken it: Nonna on the aisle with her splint in her lap and her beads in the other hand, then Rosie, Ma, Jack, Gina, and Frank on the end with his hat on his knee.

Father Dom Bruno comes out of the sacristy favoring the left knee, and he reads the Gospel with a cough drop in his cheek. Luke. *Mary set out and traveled to the hill country in haste.* At *the infant leaped in her womb* Jack has a striped blanket in his head, seven pounds three ounces, and then Father Dom is reading on.

Gina leans over in the Creed, between *one in Being with the Father* and *for us men*, and whispers, “Did you sleep?” “No.” “Me neither.” Ma looks down the pew at both of them and they say the rest of it like Catholics.
He doesn’t preach long. He never has. He stands at the ambo with both hands on it and shifts the cough drop over.

“She just got the biggest news anybody ever got,” he says. “And what does she do? Does she sit with it? She goes to see somebody. Her cousin, who’s old, and pregnant, and stuck in the hills. In haste, it says. Not when it’s convenient.” He looks out at them over his glasses. “So go see somebody this week. Somebody who’s been waiting on you. Don’t make them wait anymore.”
And he sits down. Rosie, who has been timing him on her Hannah Montana watch, holds it up to Ma: four minutes. Ma pushes her arm back down.

At Communion Nonna goes up on Frank’s arm with the splint held against her coat, and kneels after — she isn’t supposed to — and nobody stops her. Jack kneels beside Ma with his hands over his face and prays the short way, the only way he’s any good at: for the baby, by her name, the first time he’s said it to God — Lucille Odile — and for Nonna’s hand, and for Danny, and for the drive.
On the steps after, in the snow, with Frank gone ahead to start the truck, Ma buttons her coat to the top and fixes her scarf and says, without making anything of it,
“You’re coming with me. He asked.”

s05.slug: SUNDAY · 10:05 AM · TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION, THE VISITING ROOM
body: Frank takes the last row of the lot, against the fence, and leaves the engine running for the heater. The plows have been through and pushed the snow up along the chain-link in a gray wall as high as the hood, and the Cleveland station already has two men in a studio arguing about the Kansas City run defense. Ma gets the Folgers can of quarters out from under the seat and holds it in her lap with both hands.
“Tell him the twenty-seventh,” Frank says.
“You coming in, Dad?”
Frank turns the radio up a notch. “The twenty-seventh.”

The lobby is the one from Thanksgiving — the yellow cinderblock, the lockers with their red tags, the mural over them with the sun that has a face and the ducks going down to the lake — except that the officer at the desk says, “Merry Christmas, Maria,” and Ma says it back and asks after his wife’s hip by name. Coats in the locker. The stamp on the back of the hand; the two steel doors, and the wait between them.

In the visiting room somebody has cut a Christmas tree out of green construction paper and taped it to the cinderblock over the microwave, and the kids from the toy corner have colored its ornaments in crayon, one of them solid black, pressed hard. Danny comes through the far door with his hands already out: twenty-two, in the state blues, square through the shoulders, their father’s face and the gentlest eyes in the room. He gets Ma first and keeps her a while, rocking her a little on her feet, and then Jack.
“Professor.”

For twenty minutes it’s Ma’s visit. She went to the machines the minute they sat down and came back with a honey bun, and Danny ate it in three bites while she went down her list, and the wrapper is still lying open on the bolted table in front of him. Nonna’s hand, and the splint, and how she knelt at Communion this morning when she isn’t supposed to. Rosie practicing a grace for Christmas Eve in the bathroom mirror, with gestures. Gina’s grades. The baby in New Orleans, with the weight and the hour; Ma has it by heart already.
Danny looks at Jack. “The veil girl’s sister? During the *game*?”
“Third quarter. They lost after.”
“Figures.” He shakes his head at the Saints, in general.
“Dad says tell you the twenty-seventh.”
Danny looks off at the cinderblock, at about where the lot would be if the room had a window. “The twenty-seventh, Ma. All of you.” His eyes come back. “Pop too. Tell him I said.”

“I’ll tell him,” Ma says. She picks up the Folgers can and shakes it to hear what’s left. “I want a coffee.” And she goes, and takes a long time about it. She stops at a table where a woman in a church hat is visiting Reggie from Portsmouth and bends to say something that makes the woman put a hand on her arm; she gets in the line at the microwave behind two men with burritos; she admires a baby. She has not gone anywhere near the coffee.
Danny watches her go. “She does that for me too.”
He turns back to the table. “So.” He flattens the honey-bun wrapper with the side of his hand. “The O’Connor girl. Is it still something?”

“…Yeah.”

s05a.slug: SUNDAY · 10:25 AM · TRUMBULL, THE VISITING ROOM
body: He tells it with his forearms on the bolted table and his voice under the room’s. It isn’t hard. Two tables over a baby is losing an argument with a bottle, and up on the platform the officer is working through a newspaper one page at a time. He has never said any of it in order before, to anybody. Said straight through, it’s shorter than he thought it would be, and worse.

He starts with a porch in August and a girl who took his argument apart on it, and a veil at Mass the next morning — Danny has known her name since September. “She argues like it matters who’s right,” he says. “She prays at football games. Out loud.” Danny grins at the wrapper; he has had letters about the football. Then the boyfriend from home, and the night it ended, and what Jack did about it: nothing.
“I wasn’t going to be the guy waiting at the door.”
“Okay,” Danny says.
“A week later she’s seeing somebody. A guitar player. A good guy. He wrote her a song. Put her name on it.” He looks at the wrapper. “I sat through it.”
“The guitar player. You said.” Danny tips his head, their father’s move when the radio says something he doesn’t believe. “What’s it called?”
“Her name.”
“Oof,” Danny says.
“Then I disappeared. A month. I didn’t answer her. I missed the Saints.”
Danny’s eyebrows go up at the Saints. He lets Jack get to the rest.
The rest is California. “The O’Connor one. Skye.”
“What’s she do?”
“She acts.”
“Like in plays?”
“…Sort of.”
She’s funny, Jack tells him, and smart in a way that comes up behind you, and he can’t remember laughing like that with anybody. She knows about Danny, and has never made it strange.
“And she likes you?”
“She seems to.”
“Huh,” Danny says.
“We’re making it official in January.”
“Official.” Danny turns the wrapper a quarter turn on the table. “In January.”

“And the last night before the flights, it was Lena. She made a list of places, and we went to every one of them. She told me what the month looked like from her side. I said I was sorry. Not why.” He looks at his hands. “On the roof I got as far as ‘I’m in.’ Then I stopped myself.”

body.text: Somewhere in the middle of it Danny says it for him — “You’re in love with the veil girl” — and Jack doesn’t say no.

body: And the last afternoon a girl from the third floor who doesn’t believe in anything was lighting a candle at the votive rack in St. Brendan’s, and he lit one next to hers, for Danny. “She pray for me?” “She said it was research.” Danny thinks about that. “Tell her I’m a good subject.”
He stops there. Danny waits him out. The baby two tables over gives up on the bottle and falls asleep on somebody’s shoulder, and Jack gets to the part he came in here to say.
“When I’m with Skye I’m happy, Dan. I’m not faking it. I laugh all the time. I like who I am with her. And then I’m with Lena one night and it’s —”
“It’s what?”
“It’s like getting hit. And I’d go back every night.”
Danny doesn’t move. He is a man who does push-ups to think, and he has gone completely still.
Over by the microwave Ma has the sleeping baby now, handed off by its grandmother, and is walking it up and down in front of the paper tree, and isn’t looking this way at all.

s05b.slug: SUNDAY · 10:50 AM · TRUMBULL, THE VISITING ROOM
body: Danny looks at his brother across the table long enough for the officer on the platform to turn a page.
“You want me to tell you which one.”
“No.”
“Good. ’Cause I ain’t.”
“I didn’t come in here for that.”

“I know what you came in here for.” He lifts his chin at the room — the platform, the bolted chairs, the paper tree. “Look where I live, Professor. I ain’t picking nothing for nobody. Last girl I picked was Tina Mancuso, and she married a guy who sells pools.”
He puts his forearms on the table too. “I believe you. Both.”
“She said to tell you Merry Christmas,” Jack says. “Lena. With the accent.”
“So do the accent.”
“I don’t do the accent.”
“Then I didn’t get it.” But he’s grinning at the table. “She asked my name.”
In the toy corner somebody’s kid tips the bin of Duplos out onto the linoleum, and the room jumps and laughs, and Danny keeps his eyes on Jack.

He picks up the wrapper and turns it over, foil side up, and sets it down square to the edge of the table. “I ain’t gonna tell you nothing, Professor. I heard all of it.” He looks up. “So I’m gonna ask you one thing, and then Ma’s coming back with that coffee, and we’re gonna talk about Rosie.”
“Okay.”
“Which one of ’em can you tell the truth to?”
Under the bolted table Jack’s right hand closes into a fist against his knee, and opens.

The room goes on around them: the microwave, the toy corner, a woman at the next table crying a little and laughing at herself for it. Danny waits. Over at the machines a can drops into the tray, and somebody’s quarters go in after it, one at a time.

Danny nods, slow, and taps one finger on the wrapper. “Okay. That’s honest.” He lets it sit. “It ain’t an answer. Take it home.”

response: Danny lets the quiet go on. Across the room their mother has finally reached the coffee machine and is reading every button on it.
“Okay,” Danny says. “Take it with you.”

body: Ma comes back with two more honey buns, a coffee for Danny in a paper cup with playing cards printed around it, and the Folgers can a good deal lighter, and sits down into the middle of whatever this is and looks from one son to the other.
Danny takes the coffee. “He misses the beach, Ma.”

“Of course he misses the beach.” She pushes a honey bun across the table at Jack. “Eat that. You didn’t eat.” And to Danny, are they giving him the vegetables, did he get the socks, and he answers all of it, every item, and somewhere in the middle of the socks he says to Jack, “How’s the rich one?”
“LA.”
“He’ll call.”

Ma is on to the socks again, the gray wool ones, have they been through the wash yet, and Danny says yes to her and keeps his eyes on Jack. “If he comes, bring him Thursday. They stretch it for Christmas Eve — there’s an afternoon session. He’s still on my list from Thanksgiving.”
“Thursday I got seven fishes,” Ma says, not looking up.
“So send the Professor and the rich one, Ma. Pop can drive.” Danny takes the last honey bun off the table.

At a quarter to twelve the officer up on the platform calls the end of the hour, and the room stands up with all its chairs. The hug at the end is allowed. Danny gives Ma hers, and then he has Jack by both shoulders at arm’s length and takes a good look at him.
“Professor. You walked in here like it’s confession.”
“It was.”
“Yeah?” Danny lets go. “Penance is you come back the twenty-seventh and act normal in front of Ma.”
He goes out through the far door with the other men in blue, and at the door he turns and points at Ma, and she points back.

Out in the lot the truck is where they left it, running, a skin of new snow over the windshield except for two clear half-moons the defroster has worked open at the bottom of the glass. Frank has the pregame up. He waits till Ma’s door shuts, and puts it in reverse.

The space heater glows orange on the concrete and the Stroh’s fridge hums against the back wall, and on the workbench the radio has the Browns in Kansas City on the Cleveland station, at a volume Ma can hear through two doors. Somebody — Frank will not discuss who — has run a strand of colored lights along the pegboard over the bench, looped between the coffee can of drywall screws and the vise. Jack has the chair with the duct tape on the seat; he came straight out here from the truck at one and hasn’t gone in, and his father hasn’t asked him to. Frank has the bucket, turned over, and the thermos, and when he pours, the steam comes up off the lid smelling of Folgers. The door of the Stroh’s fridge hasn’t opened all afternoon.

It has been an afternoon. Cribbs has taken two kickoffs back for touchdowns, the second one a hundred and three yards, and the man on the radio still hasn’t got his voice back from it. Frank came up off the bucket for that one and put his head into the colored lights, and the noise brought Gina to the side door in her socks. “Ma says this isn’t a bar.” “Tell your mother a hundred and three.” “I don’t know what that means.” “She will.” Jerome Harrison has been running all day through a Kansas City defense that seems to have gone home at the half, and every time the radio gives his yards Frank says a number under his breath. “Two-thirty-seven.” Jim Brown’s. In the fourth quarter Harrison goes past it, and Frank quits saying it and just sits forward on the bucket with his elbows on his knees, his lips moving with the down and distance. Somewhere in the third quarter Jack noticed he was laughing too, at a Browns game, in December, and he can’t say when it started.

With forty-four seconds left Harrison goes twenty-eight yards for the score, and the radio loses its mind, and it’s Browns 41, Chiefs 34. Frank stands up off the bucket with the thermos lid in his hand.
“Two-eighty-six.”
That’s the call. Then he laughs — head back, at the colored lights, with coffee going over the rim of the lid onto his boot.

response: Frank looks down at the thermos.
“Your mother asked me. I said Christmas.” He screws the cap back on, all the way down, and sets it on the bench under the lights. “We’ll see about after.”

choices.text: *Take the coffee he pours you. Say nothing about it.*
response: Frank fills the lid again and holds it out without asking, and Jack takes it. They pass it back and forth, two men and one thermos lid, while the radio gives them the run twice more in the highlights, and both times Frank says the number along with it.

choices.text: “Two-eighty-six. They’ll put him on a stamp.”
response: “They’ll trade him by March.” Frank sits back down on the bucket, still grinning, and pours.

The shortest day of the year doesn’t bother getting light. At twenty to noon the window over the sink is gray, and the snow along the curb on Glenwood has gone gray to match, and Ma has the light on over the stove like it’s February.

He and his father shoveled the walk at eight, and the Kovacs’ next door, and Mrs. Pavlik’s across the street because her son is in Columbus, without discussing any of it, and came in with their faces burning. He slept in Danny’s bed again and woke at six to the plow going by.

Rosie is at the other end of the table making a paper chain out of strips of construction paper, one link for every day left till Christmas; she ran out of days at four and is making more links anyway, for after. In the front room Nonna has the Rosary going on EWTN and is praying a decade behind it. Gina is still asleep. Ursuline let out Friday, and Gina has explained to everybody that break is a sacrament.
He texted Margot happy birthday at nine. She answered at 9:02.

body: Ma is at the table with her coffee and the envelope from Saturday night. It has run out of back and started down the front. Jack is eating the last of the wedding soup for breakfast because it was there.
“Gina says you sleep with that phone.”
“Gina sleeps with a Jonas Brother.”
“That’s a *poster*.”
“She talks to it.”
Ma looks at him over her glasses, and at the RAZR face-down by his bowl, and leaves it lying there. She has never picked it up. She writes *cardoons* on the envelope and underlines it twice.
At 11:52 it buzzes against the oilcloth, and the little outer screen says THEO.
He has it open on the first ring.
“You answered,” Theo says, at once — and from the sound of it he had a voicemail ready, with an introduction.

response: “I tell you a lot of things, Costigan. You’ve never done one of them.” A breath, out in Brentwood. “Don’t make a habit of it. I’ll have nothing to talk about.”
“Your conscience,” Theo says. “Calling from Brentwood. I have a request.”
Theo clears his throat, out in Brentwood. “I had a preamble. Four minutes. There was a joke about my mother’s life coach’s life coach.”
“Come for Christmas.”
“…Yes,” Theo says. “That’s what I was calling about. You’ve ruined the preamble.”

body: The preamble comes anyway, because Theo can’t help it: there is a man coming to his mother’s house on the twenty-sixth to move the furniture for spiritual reasons; and he would like — only if it’s no trouble, and he can tell from here that it’s trouble — to come to Youngstown for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. “Just the two days. I’ll be out of your hair by Saturday. Your father won’t have to see me in daylight more than twice.”
Jack lowers the phone. “Ma. Theo wants to know can he come Christmas Eve. And Christmas.”

Ma takes the RAZR out of his hand. She doesn’t put it to her ear so much as speak down into it, like the intercom at St. Brigid’s school. “Theo? Honey. *You come.*” She listens; Jack can hear Theo through the little speaker saying *Mrs. Costigan* the way other people say *Your Holiness*. “No. No. You come.” She hands it back and writes THEO on the envelope, under the smelts.
“Tell him we sit down at twenty to seven,” she says to Jack, “and we don’t wait for anybody. Not the Pope.”
Frank is in the side doorway in his Carhartt, with snow on his boots and an orange extension cord over his shoulder, on his way back out to the garage. He doesn’t come in.
“Tell him he don’t call first.”
“He called first, Dad.”
“Tell him anyway.” And he’s gone back across the yard with the cord paying out behind him.

“I heard,” Theo says in Jack’s ear. “Tell him —” and stops, and starts again, a man who has the end of every sentence and doesn’t have the end of this one. “Tell him thank you.” He recovers. “Eight-oh-nine Thursday morning. A gate with a letter in it. I’ll be the one in a coat that’s wrong for Ohio.”

“Danny wants you Thursday,” Jack says. “Christmas Eve. They do a holiday visit in the afternoon. You’re still on his list.” A leaf blower starts up somewhere behind him in Brentwood. “Then I’ll need to know what you wear to a prison on Christmas Eve,” Theo says. “Something that isn’t the coat.” “It’s the parka. It’s always the parka.” “Of course it is.”
“And tell your grandmother her twenty is guarding 412,” Theo says. “I left it in charge.”
When they’ve hung up, Nonna wants to know from the front room who that was. Ma tells her *il ricco*. Nonna smooths the gray cashmere over her knees with her left hand. “*Lo sapevo.*”
It’s full dark by a quarter past five. At 6:05, when the sun is just down in New Orleans:

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol.

body: At ten to one the RAZR goes on the nightstand, and the outer screen says LENA, and it isn’t a text.
“Are you asleep?” she says.
“No.”

“Good. Me neither.” There’s nothing behind her at all — no television, no Tony, no screen door; a ceiling fan turning over, in December. “Everybody on Dupre Street is asleep. Tess sent eleven pictures of the same baby and went to bed. I’ve been lying here since eleven with the Holy See on my mind, and I told you to pick a side by kickoff, and you didn’t.”

He sits up against the headboard of Danny’s bed. The alley light comes through the blind in slats. “Venerable’s too soon,” he says. “Open the archives first. If he was a saint in 1942, it’ll still be true when they’ve read his mail.”

“Golda Meir,” Lena says. “1958. ‘When fearful martyrdom came to our people, the voice of the Pope was raised for the victims.’ She was Israel’s foreign minister. You’re a freshman. And the Chief Rabbi of Rome got baptized after the war and took his *name*, Jack. Eugenio. You don’t take the name of a man who stood around.”
“He was quiet in 1942. Prudent, fine. Venerable means heroic.”

“Prudence *is* heroic. It’s a cardinal virtue; it’s on the same list as your fortitude, look it up.” The fan turns over. “You want him to have said something loud in 1942 so you can feel better about him in 2009. That isn’t his virtue you’re grading. That’s yours.”
He opens his mouth, and there isn’t anything in it. On Dupre Street she waits him out. He can hear her smiling; he could pick it out of a recording.
“Say it,” she says.
“That’s a point.”
“That’s *the* point. I’ll take it.” And then she gives a little back. “They should open the archives. I told Daddy so. He says I’m a modernist.”
“Where’s the 8-Ball?”

“On the nightstand. It said *very doubtful* and then we lost. I’m keeping it for a prophet.” The slosh of blue water, close to the phone. “Is Pius going to be a saint?” A pause while it surfaces. “*Cannot predict now*.”
“That’s the Holy See’s position too.”
“Don’t you make me laugh. Mama’s through the wall.”

She tells him the rest of her Monday: the baby home from Touro, Mémère supervising the car seat in French and Beau carrying the diaper bag like it might go off; Josie’s list of names for the baby’s first dog. “Julian sent Mémère a Christmas card,” she says. “From Oakland. With a flower in it, pressed, from his mother’s garden. She has it on the icebox next to the Pope.”
Jack lies back down on Danny’s pillow and looks at the slats on the ceiling.
“I’m in Danny’s bed,” he says. He doesn’t know he’s going to say it till it’s out. “Mine’s three feet away. I’ve slept in his every night since Sunday.”
The fan turns over on Dupre Street. She doesn’t ask him why.
“Then sleep in it,” she says. “Somebody ought to.”

After that they talk about nothing. Rosie’s paper chain, out of days and still going. Whether a bathtub Mary counts as a grotto: she says yes; he says it’s a bathtub. It’s past one, then half past. Twice she says she’s going to let him sleep, and then tells him something else.
At a quarter to two her voice has gone low and slow at the edges, and the fan is louder than she is.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 2:00 PM · THE SOUTHERN PARK MALL
body: Frank lets them out at the department-store doors with the engine running and says four o’clock, and says it again through the window. Inside, with three shopping days left, all of Mahoning County has had the same idea at once. Gina has sixty dollars of babysitting money folded small in her coat pocket and her hand on it. She waits for the escalator.
“Twenty-seven days.” She is looking straight up at the top of it. “Do you know how hard that is? I go to *Ursuline*.”
“I know.”
“You don’t *know*.” At the top she steps off and turns around. “Is she nice?”
“No.”
“Good.” Three stores later, in front of a window full of mannequins in scarves: “Is she the nice one in real life?”
“She’s the other one.”
“*Good*.”

Past the Hallmark store she starts up again without warning, low, steering around strollers. “I almost told Kelsey. I told Kelsey I *almost* told her something, and now she follows me around like I’m a raffle. Ma came down Thursday while it was on and asked what I was watching, and I said *nothing*. With it *on*.” She looks at him at last, outraged. “*Nothing*, Jack.”

She lets that carry them to the food court. In line at the pretzel stand, reading the board, she says, “You said the nun’s name like seven times at the kitchen table Saturday,” and that’s all she does with it. She orders a cinnamon one and splits it with him.

At the Orange Julius Ashley Vrabel is in line with her mother, in a Penn State sweatshirt. Gina sees her first. She lifts a hand about shoulder high, and Ashley glances at her mother, and lifts one back. When they’re past, Gina says, “We’re not friends. We’re *Catholic*.”

The gifts take an hour. For Theo, a Browns knit hat of his own, orange, the same as Frank’s — “So he quits borrowing Dad’s stuff,” Gina says. For Rosie he picks a stuffed crab up off a pile of them, and Gina says, “Do *not* say Idaho,” and he puts it back and buys the sixty-four colored markers that come in a tin. For Nonna, fleece slippers with backs that fold down. For Ma, the good hand cream. For Frank, a snow brush; the one behind the seat is held together with tape. Gina buys something flat in a bag, for him, and won’t let him see it, and carries it against her chest. Hers he’ll have to come back for alone, and she knows it, and walks him past the earrings twice.

By the Santa line the Altar and Rosary ladies from a Slovak parish in Campbell have a card table of nut rolls and cookbooks. Gina stops across from them at a kiosk of calendars and looks at a calendar of puppies, hard.
“Are you getting the nun something?”

response: It’s eight dollars, *Our Favorite Recipes*, with pierogi on page forty-one three different ways and a note at the bottom from a Mrs. Hudak about the dough. He borrows a pen from the ladies and writes on the inside cover, in capitals: *PROOF. —J.*
Gina reads it over his arm. “That’s it? That’s the letter?”
“That’s the letter.”
She thinks about it, and nods, a professional.

response: It’s been in his inside pocket since breakfast, one of Ma’s box of parish cards with the stained-glass Brigid on the front. He wrote his line at the kitchen table, and while it was still out of the envelope Nonna had the pen out of his hand and was writing under it, slanted, in the hand they taught in San Giovanni in Fiore.
“What did she write?” Gina says.
“*Buon Natale alla suora.*”
“She calls her the nun in *writing*?”
“No,” he says.
Gina puts the puppies back. “Coward.”

body: At half past three Gina goes into a store that sells nothing but candles, and he tells her he’ll wait outside, and crosses Market Street at the light to the post office.
The line is out the door, people holding boxes against their chests with both arms, and it doesn’t move, and then it does.

body: At the window a clerk in a pair of light-up antlers sells him a money order for forty dollars. He fills it out at the counter by the pens on their chains and addresses a plain envelope in block capitals — D. KOSTELNIK, and a street, and STRUTHERS, OHIO — with no return address, and puts it through the slot marked LOCAL. “Merry Christmas,” the clerk says, and her antlers blink. Struthers is eleven minutes from where he’s standing. He has never driven it.
Frank is at the doors at four. Gina gets in the middle without being told.

At home there is a box under the tree that wasn’t there this morning, out in front of the Nativity: a Priority Mail box with a round black postmark — MARISOL CA, DEC 17 — and the return address in tall, even capitals, N. DUPRE ST., NEW ORLEANS, LA. Ma is standing over it with the dish towel on her shoulder, and from the tape at the corners it’s been picked up and put back down more than once.
“From California,” Ma says. “Who in California sends you a *package*?”
“Lena.”
Behind him on the mat Gina takes her boots off one at a time, very slowly, listening.
At six, with the box still sitting unopened in front of the Nativity where Ma can keep an eye on it, the phone goes on the stairs.

At twenty to three the RAZR goes off on the nightstand in Danny’s room, rattling against the wood beside the lamp, and Jack has it in his fist on the first buzz. The outer screen says SKYE (MISFIT). It lights the crucifix over the door and the trophy on Danny’s shelf, the little gold man with his arm snapped off.

He takes it down the stairs barefoot, in the Carhartt over his pajama pants, and the seventh stair tells the house about it, as it always has. The house sleeps through it. His father is snoring in two parts behind the bedroom door; the lamp is off in the front room where Nonna sleeps in her chair. The phone stops on the stairs. It starts again in the kitchen. At the top of the basement steps, with the door pulled to behind him, he has two bars, which is where the house keeps them, and he opens it.
“No,” Jack says.

A party comes down the line from a long way off: a bass line, mostly, thudding through canvas. “You’re saying no to a *phone*, Jack,” Skye says. “It’s just me. I’m at the bottom of a driveway. The party’s at the top. I came down here where it’s only the car.”

He goes down in the dark to the bottom step and sits. The Dell is on where Gina left it on the card table, its fan whining, the screen saver throwing a slow blue drift across the paneling. Behind him the furnace lights with a thump and settles into its run. Ma’s laundry baskets, the old Zenith under a bedsheet, and in the laundry sink, under a dinner plate with a can of Contadina on it to keep it down, a slab of salt cod the size of a hymnal lying in water gone cloudy.
“Where are you?” she says. “Be specific.”
“The basement. The furnace. My sister’s computer.”
“What does it smell like?”
He breathes in, and regrets it. “Salt cod. Soaking.”
“Since when?”
“Monday.”
“Jack,” Skye says. “That’s a hostage situation.”
“My grandmother’s orders. My mother changes the water twice a day.”

“And it’s still in there. Breathing.” The bass thuds on. “I’m in a dress I can’t sit down in, so I’m lying across both seats with my shoes on the dashboard, in case you were picturing it. You were picturing it.” He was. “So,” she says. “A funny thing happened at a party.”

And she does a voice. A young man’s voice, unhurried, every vowel paid for in advance: *“I’m here strictly as a favor. There’s a woman named Pilar who does my mother’s eyebrows, and her nephew’s girlfriend went to Crossroads with the host, and Pilar said go, be seen, it’s Christmas — and I owe Pilar for a thing in 2006 that I can’t get into.”* After it, a little intake of air, held: the half second before the bow. Jack has watched it in doorways and dining rooms since August. He knows the voice before she says a name. He knows it from the eyebrows.
“Your roommate,” Skye says, herself again, “was being extremely odd tonight. Even for him.”
He hasn’t said a word. The furnace runs.
“I did your professor off a description,” she says. “I’ve had *years* of Ted.”
“Ted.”

“Ted. Theo, to you people. Since we were eleven.” The seat creaks under her. “His father’s company makes my show. Meridian — it’s at the end of every episode, after the caterer. Same sets. Same wrap parties. Every wrap party from sixth grade on, I was under the craft-services table with Ted, rating everybody’s outfits. We’re practically siblings. The bad kind. The kind who’ve seen each other at their worst.” A pause with bass in it. “I was sick on his shoes when I was fourteen and I will not be discussing it.”
“Do him,” she says. “You live with him. Say *strictly*.”
“I can’t do voices.”
“Everybody can do Ted. Say it.”
“Strictly,” Jack says.
“That’s a man buying a boat,” Skye says. “That’s a dentist buying a boat. Never do that again.”
“His father calls him Teddy.”
“I know,” Jack says. “I saw the card.”
“Then you know why I don’t. I’m the only one who calls him Ted.” Something rustles — her coat, the seat belt. “At the Hallorans’, I saw him walk in. With you. I got behind a ficus.”
“A ficus.”
“A big one. I’m a professional.”
“Too many people you went to middle school with,” he says.

“One,” Skye says. “Mostly one. And at Ellery — you told me your roommate asked why you looked like you’d been through a war. *Tell him it was a peace mission.* That was me waving at Ted over your head.” She doesn’t wait for him to ask the next part. “You want to know why I didn’t say. Because you’d have asked him about me. And he’d have told you the truth, and I wanted you to find it out slower.”
On the Dell twelve feet from where he’s sitting, the Sunday after Thanksgiving, it said *1 mutual friend: Theo Vance*, and he read it as Theo knowing everybody.

“Tonight,” she says, “I’m out on a terrace hiding from a hot tub, and he comes out through the slider, and he sees me, and he stops. He looks at me like he’s doing long division.” The voice again, lower, without the eyebrows in it: *“Callender. You’re in Marisol.”* Herself: “Since November.” Him: *“Since the Hallorans’. That ficus had your shoes.”*

“He had on the camel coat. It was fifty-five degrees on that terrace with a heat lamp going. Ted only wears a coat to a party he means to leave early, so he can leave holding something.” She clicks her tongue. “He wasn’t asking,” Skye says. “He knows, Jack. He’s known since your Thanksgiving — he has to have. I friended you on a Wednesday, and Ted reads Facebook like it’s the trades and pretends he’s above it.” The seat creaks again; she’s sat up. “Here’s the part. Ted has never been careful with me in his life. He tells me I’ve got lipstick on my teeth in front of casting directors. He told me my first boyfriend looked like a thumb. Tonight he was careful. With every word. Ted’s only careful when he’s protecting somebody.”
She doesn’t say who.

“And then he goes,” and she’s him once more, the last of it: *“What are you doing, Callender?”* Herself: “I never know what I’m doing, Ted.” And Ted, gently, on his way back in through the slider: *“He does. That’s the problem.”*
Up at the top of the driveway somebody changes the song. She doesn’t add anything to it. In the laundry sink the plate on the baccalà ticks once against the porcelain as the furnace shakes the floor.

s08a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:00 AM · THE BASEMENT → THE SIDE YARD
body: “He’s coming here,” Jack says. “Christmas Eve. He called Monday and asked.”

Down the line something gets knocked — the gearshift, from the clunk of it. “To your *house*?” Skye says. “Oh, he’s going to be *so polite*. He’s going to bring your mother something in a box she’s afraid to open.”
“Balsamic. At Thanksgiving. In velvet.”
“Of *course* in velvet.” She’s rocking the car; the canvas creaks in its frame. “I would give a kidney to see Ted in a house where everybody shares a bathroom.”
“There’s a hook on the door.”
“Seventeen days,” she says. “I’m not counting. You said yes. I wrote it on my hand. It’s still there; I’m a terrible bather.”
Somebody comes down the driveway past her car, laughing, and goes back up. She waits for them to go.
“I’d rather be in your basement,” she says.
“It smells like fish.”
“Then I’d rather be in your basement with you in it.”

The furnace cuts out. In the quiet the Dell’s fan sounds like a small plane. He sits on the bottom step with the phone against his ear and the concrete under his heels, and doesn’t have anything smart to say. On her end, nothing either; the bass, and her breathing.
“Is it snowing there?” she says.
“It snowed Saturday.”
“So there’s snow.”
“There’s old snow.”
“Are you wearing shoes?”
“No.”
“Good. Don’t. Go stand in it.” And when he laughs: “I’m serious. Go outside and do the weather. Like the girl on the eleven o’clock. You have a girl on the eleven o’clock.”
“Everybody has a girl on the eleven o’clock.”
“Then be her. Go.”

He goes. Up the basement steps, across the kitchen linoleum in the dark, and out the side door, and the spring takes the door out of his hand and slams it behind him like a shot, loud enough for every house on Glenwood Avenue, and he stands on the step with the phone at his ear, waiting for a light to come on upstairs. None does.

The side yard is three days of snow gone hard on top, gray at the edges where the plow threw the street up onto it. The first step holds him. The second goes through the crust to the ankle, and both feet are on fire at once, and then they’re just gone. That’s easier. Frank’s blue lights are wound around the tub at the back of the yard, and the Madonna stands in it with the snow on her frozen to a glaze, the lights making her blue all the way up.
“Five-day,” Skye says. “Give me a high. Point at something.”

He points at the Madonna. “Good morning,” he says. “It’s five past three on Glenwood Avenue. Here at the Costigan station the Blessed Mother is reporting three days of accumulation, holding steady, under blue lights.”
“Turn to camera. Smile like you’re paid.”
He turns to camera, which is the neighbors’ garage. “Two doors up, an inflatable Santa remains on his face. Three days. No change in his condition.”
“Hand out. Show me a front.”

He shows her a front. Out of the dryer vent by the side door the furnace’s breath comes up white and rolls off along the siding, and he puts it in the forecast. He sweeps his free arm from the neighbors’ to the alley pole. “Thursday, clear. A high in the thirties. Christmas, I can’t help you with Christmas. Christmas is out of my hands.” He looks up, where the moon would be. “And no moon tonight, folks. None at all. Somebody took it.”
“Do the Madonna,” Skye says. “From the top. I fell asleep before you finished her.”

“My grandfather dug her in before I was born. A clawfoot tub, on its end, painted blue inside. She’s concrete. She weighs more than my father.” He points, weather-girl, at the blue. “Light accumulation in both hands.”

Skye is laughing so hard the horn goes off at her end, a short honk at the bottom of a driveway in the hills, and she says *sorry, sorry* to whoever’s up there, and keeps laughing. And so is he, barefoot to the shins in old snow in his pajama pants at five past three in the morning, with his breath going up in the alley light and one arm out showing a girl in California a cold front over Brownlee Woods, laughing so his ribs hurt and he has to bend over his knees, and nothing in him wants to be anywhere but here.
“Go to bed, Ohio,” Skye says when she can. “Next time I call, you’re doing the five-day.”
She hangs up.
On the kitchen linoleum his feet are red to the ankle.
Wednesday the light goes off Glenwood a little before five. At six Ma is down at the laundry sink giving the baccalà its last water, and Jack is on the top step with the RAZR, where the bars are.

s09.slug: THURSDAY · 6:55 AM · THE SILVERADO, ROUTE 60 SOUTH → PITTSBURGH INTERNATIONAL
body: Christmas Eve starts black and clear over Beaver County, the stars still out over the hills and the road dry for the first time since Saturday, white with salt in the headlights. Frank had them out of the driveway at a quarter past six. The heater is still making up its mind. On the bench seat, folded square in the place where a third person would sit, is the Browns parka — orange and brown, older than Gina, the cuff mended with electrical tape. Frank carried it out of the garage in the dark and put it there before Jack came out of the house with the thermos.

KDKA is on low: the airport weather, the Parkway, a man who wants them to know about a mattress sale on the twenty-sixth. A few minutes past seven the newsman stops reading traffic. The Senate, he says, has passed the health-care bill, sixty to thirty-nine, in a vote taken at seven o’clock this morning — the first time the Senate has voted on Christmas Eve since 1895 — with the Vice President in the chair and not one Republican for it.
Frank listens to the end of it with his thumb still on the wheel.
“Merry Christmas,” Frank says.
“They bought Nebraska,” Jack says. “And the Senate wrote something that sounds like Stupak’s language and isn’t. They’ll find a way to pay for abortions with it. They always find a way.”
Frank drives. Off to the left, behind the hills, the sky has started to go gray.

“Your grandmother’s hand,” he says. “Medicare. And it still sent a bill with a comma in it. It’s on the kitchen table, under your mother’s list.” He checks the mirror. “Stupak’s a good man. They’ll beat him for it.” A salt truck, and Frank goes around it on the left with no blinker, there being no blinker on that side. “Nebraska gets something. The insurance guys get something. Some guy laid off in Lordstown whose kid gets sick gets something.” He settles back into the right lane. “Everybody gets something.”
Jack has an answer for that, and the answer to the answer, and drinks his coffee instead.

At ten after eight the sun is up pink over the long-term lots and Pittsburgh International is full of people trying to get somewhere by tonight. Frank took the parka off the seat when they parked and carried it in over his arm. Theo comes down the escalator into baggage claim in the camel coat with a garment bag over one shoulder and a Neiman Marcus bag in the other hand, unshaven, the red-eye gray under both eyes and in the hair he hasn’t done anything about. He sees them at the bottom and puts on charming somewhere around the middle of the escalator.
Frank hands him the parka without a word. Theo sets the Neiman Marcus bag down on the tile and puts the parka on over the camel coat without one, and picks the bag back up.

In the truck Theo gets in the middle, with the garment bag laid across his knees and Jack’s, and by the time they’re down out of the parking garage he’s talking. He saw *Avatar* three times in four days, in IMAX, in the glasses. “Once for the story. Twice for the floating mountains. You have to see the mountains twice or they don’t count.” His mother’s life coach has acquired a life coach; they disagreed about his mother in front of her, at dinner.

body: Christmas Eve at his father’s in Brentwood would have been a caterer and a tree delivered already decorated, in a color the decorator called *oyster*.
“Oyster,” Frank says.
“A kind of beige, sir. With ambitions.”
“I hear the Browns won something, sir.”
Frank keeps his eyes on the road. “Two-eighty-six. Harrison. Other kid took a kickoff back a hundred and three. Chiefs went home at the half.”
“Two-eighty-six,” Theo says, trying it.
Frank looks over at him. “Close.”
Jack watches Theo work: the timing, the detail stacked on detail, every line built for an audience that hasn’t been told how this ends. Jack has been told. He lets him do it anyway.
At the merge onto Route 60 Theo runs out, or lets himself run out, and looks through the windshield at the hills going by with the old snow on them.
“How’s Ohio?”
“Cold.”

Theo looks out at the fields — white, the fences drawn across them in black, a barn with a lit star on its peak in the daylight — and doesn’t push, and Jack doesn’t give, and that rides along with them to the state line like a fourth passenger with its knees up.

s10.slug: THURSDAY · 10:30 AM · ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE, THE CONFESSION LINE
body: On Christmas Eve morning the line for confession at St. Brigid’s runs down the side aisle from the fifth Station to the second, and it’s half the South Side: women in their good parkas with their purses held in both hands, a man in a union jacket reading the bulletin like a racing form, two Mooney sophomores somebody’s mother has marched over, shoving each other in whispers. Up front the Holy Name men are on ladders, hanging garland off the choir loft and arguing about the staple gun. Mrs. Pallante from the school cafeteria turns around in line, sees him, tells him he got tall, and turns back.

The confessional is the old one, built into the wall between the Stations: dark oak gone black at the edges where hands push the curtains back, a velvet curtain on either side, and over the middle door, where the priest sits, a small light, green, which means Father’s in.
A week ago Wednesday he told a priest in California he’d go Christmas Eve, at home.

The left-hand curtain slides back and an old man comes out putting his cap on. The woman ahead of Jack goes in, and it’s him next, standing under the green light with his hands in the Carhartt’s pockets and the line at his back.

s10a.slug: THURSDAY · 10:50 AM · ST. BRIGID’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: He draws the curtain to behind him and kneels in the dark. It smells of varnish and wet wool and somebody’s Jean Naté. The kneeler is worn into two shallow dips by other people’s knees. At the height of his face there’s a brass grille with a cloth behind it, and behind the cloth a shape, a chair creaking, a cough drop clicking against teeth. Somewhere in the wall a radiator is coming up, ticking in the pipe, a small dry knock every few seconds. The little door behind the grille slides open.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been eight days since my last confession.”

Through the curtain he can hear the line breathing: a purse clasp, one of the sophomores getting shushed, somebody’s beads knocking a pew end. He had it in order coming down Glenwood. On the kneeler it comes out in whatever order it likes.
“There’s a girl. At school, in California.” On the other side of the cloth Father Dom breathes through his nose and waits.
“She sent me a picture on my phone. Of herself. I opened it. And I kept it.”
“A week ago, in her car.” He says the rest of that one to the grille. “I was the one who went too far this time.”
“This time,” Father Dom says.
“Usually she’s the one driving.”
“And I took a minute I shouldn’t have. Before I stopped. I knew I was taking it.”
“Did it stop?” Father Dom says. “In the car.”
“It stopped.”
“Good.”

“And Father, one more thing. It’s an errand.” Jack has it by heart. “A priest in California said to tell you you’re very lucky to have me in your line. And very sorry.” Behind the grille the cough drop goes over to the other cheek. “Tell him we’ll see.”
“For these and all my sins I’m sorry.”
The chair creaks while Father Dom gets the knee straightened out under him.
“You’re home,” he says, “and she’s in California. God gave you two thousand miles for Christmas. Don’t mail them back.”

The cough drop clicks. “Thirty years I’ve had men off the line at Lordstown in this box. Not one of them ever told me he decided to drink the house payment. He stopped for one on the way home, one Friday. Then it was Fridays. Pretty soon it was the way home.” A pause. “The old books call it the near occasion. You don’t beat it every Friday. You take a different street.”
“For your penance, help your mother with the fish. All seven.” Another click. “And a rosary for the girl. By her name. For her, not for you.”

response: “I’ll keep the miles,” Jack says.
“Keep every one of them.”

“Pray for her, Father.”
“What’s her name?”
“Skye.”
Behind the grille there’s a pause, and a creak that might be the knee. “I will.”

body: He says the Act of Contrition as they all learned it for First Confession, *O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended Thee*, right through to *amend my life*, and behind the cloth the shadow of Father Dom’s hand comes up.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“Go in peace.”
The radiator in the wall knocks twice and goes quiet.

Out on the steps the sky has been scraped clean overnight, hard blue from the steeple to the Valley, and the old snow on the lawns along Glenwood has gone to crust that shines. He goes down the street toward the house with his hands in the Carhartt’s pockets, counting off the first decade on his fingers inside the left one, and into every Hail Mary, under his breath, he puts her name.

s10c.slug: THURSDAY · 1:05 PM · TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION, THE VISITING ROOM
body: Frank takes the last row of the lot again, against the same gray wall of plowed snow, and leaves the engine running, and doesn’t say *the twenty-seventh*, because it’s understood. Theo gets out of the truck in the Browns parka over the camel coat with the hood down and stands a second looking at the fence, at the coils along the top of it lit up silver in the clear, and then he follows Jack in.

The lobby on Christmas Eve is a waiting room at a bus station the day before a holiday. Every plastic chair is taken. Somebody has hung a paper chain along the top of the lockers, and somebody else has put a Santa hat on the officer at the desk, who wears it the way he wears the badge: straight, and without comment. Theo signs the visitor log in fountain-pen ink and hands his license across without being asked, and the officer runs a finger down a list and finds him. “Vance. You’re approved.” Coats in the lockers; phones in the lockers. The stamp on the back of the hand. In the space between the two steel doors Theo puts his hand on the cinderblock.

The visiting room is loud with it — kids in their good clothes, grandmothers, a man in state blues holding a baby up over his head at the end of his arms while the baby shrieks with joy. The paper tree is still taped up over the microwave. Danny comes through the far door and finds them first.
“Professor.” And then, to Theo, with a look at the parka: “You came back.”
“Your father said I didn’t have to call first.”

Danny stops halfway into the bolted chair. “He said that?” Behind him a C.O. on the platform calls a name, and a woman two tables down gets up with both hands over her mouth. “He never said that to nobody.”

Theo has a roll of quarters in his fist from the truck, and he’s at the machines while Danny is still sitting down. Danny watches him go. “What’d I tell him about buying?” “He says Christmas Eve is a loophole.” “He would.” Theo comes back with a honey bun, two coffees in the paper cups with the playing cards around them, and a bag of Funyuns he sets down in front of Danny with both hands.

For an hour Jack mostly listens. Danny wants the Browns from somebody who was there for it. Jack tells him Sunday in the garage — Cribbs, a hundred and three, the thermos, Gina in her socks at the side door — and Theo, who could not have told a first down from a fumble at Thanksgiving and heard it once this morning from the man himself, does the *two-eighty-six* in Frank’s exact voice. “Do it again,” Danny says. Theo does it again. Danny tells them Christmas inside: the chaplain’s Mass at eight tomorrow, the turkey roll, Reggie from Portsmouth teaching the whole unit the words to “Feliz Navidad” so he can lead it badly. Theo tells him he’s been learning the seven fishes since ten this morning from a woman who won’t speak English to him on principle.
“She’s gonna put the eel on you tonight,” Danny says. “Watch. She puts it right on your plate. Pop won’t touch it. Twenty-four years.”
“Is there a technique?”
“Yeah. Don’t think.” Danny grins. “I never ate it once. Tell Nonna I said you’re a coward if you don’t.”
Somewhere in the second coffee Theo turns his cup around once on the bolted table and says, mildly, to nobody in particular: “Has he told you about California?”
Danny doesn’t look at Jack. Not once. “He told me he misses the beach.”
Theo looks at Danny for a second, and then at Jack, and then back down at his coffee with the playing cards printed around it. “It’s a very good beach,” he says.
Near the end the room starts to stand up in pieces, people reaching for each other before they’re told. Danny leans in on his forearms. “Nonna still praying for you?”
“Since Thanksgiving. She says starting that night.”
“Then you’re covered, man. She don’t miss.” He gives Theo a long plain look. “Thanksgiving I said somebody oughta come see you. So who comes to see you, out there?”
Theo opens his mouth on something ready, and it doesn’t come. He tips his head at Jack. “He does. He doesn’t knock.”
“Good,” Danny says.

At five to three the officer calls the end of it. The hug at the end is allowed. Danny gets Jack first, a hand on the back of his head like when they were kids, and then he gets Theo too, without asking, both arms, and Theo, who shakes hands with everybody’s father and bows from the waist to girls in doorways, stands inside it with his own hands up in the air like a man at a stickup before he puts them down on Danny’s back.
“Merry Christmas, rich one.”
“Merry Christmas, Danny.”

Out in the lot the windshield has fogged from the inside and Frank has the Cleveland station on, two men already arguing about Oakland on Sunday. Theo gets in the middle. Past the fence the fields are white on both sides, the stubble coming up through the snow in rows.
“Mr. Costigan,” Theo says. “What was Danny like at eleven?”
Frank drives. Jack thinks he isn’t going to answer.
“Same,” Frank says. “Ate everything.” He moves the truck over for a plow. “Laughed at his own jokes before he got to the end of them.”

By four the kitchen windows have steamed over from the inside, and the radio on top of the refrigerator — Nonna’s, tuned since before Jack was born to the AM station out of Warren that plays the Italian Christmas records all day on the twenty-fourth — has come around to the donkey.

The baccalà is up out of the basement sink at last and simmering in Ma’s tomatoes with the olives. The clams wait in a colander for the linguine. On the back of the counter, coiled in a Pyrex dish under foil where Frank won’t have to look at it, is the eel — *capitone*. Nonna has put it on this table every Christmas Eve since 1951, and Frank has refused it every Christmas Eve since he married in. He has been out in the garage since three.

Theo is at the sink in the ST. BRIGID’S FISH FRY 2006 apron with the sleeves of a navy sweater shoved up past his elbows, cleaning squid. Nonna is directing from her chair in the kitchen doorway, where Frank carried it for her after lunch, with her beads in her left hand, and she is not satisfied. She says something in Calabrese, at length.
“She says you hold it like a baby you don’t like,” Gina says from the table, where she has her hands in the dough for the bread with the anchovies baked in.

“I hold all babies like this,” Theo says. “Ask my sister.” He turns the squid over, draws the quill out of it, clear as a strip of cellophane, and holds it up toward the doorway for inspection. Nonna gives it a nod.

He has been learning the rules since ten, with two hours off for Trumbull, and has come back from it needing to be useful. Seven fishes: never six, never eight. No meat in the house till midnight, not even for the dog — there is no dog; Nonna is speaking generally. The anchovies in the bread count as a fish, whatever Danny used to say about it. You don’t sit down at the table before Nonna sits. And the eel isn’t one of the seven. Gina, asked to translate why, consulted Nonna and came back with it: “It’s a penance. For the men.”

Rosie is kneeling on a chair at the counter doing the donkey along with the radio — she has had the donkey’s part by heart since she was four — and she has been teaching it to Theo, who learns it the way he learns everything, too fast and with questions. “Is he an Italian donkey?” “He’s from *Italy*,” Rosie says, appalled. Theo does the donkey. He does it well. Gina stops kneading. “I’m going to die in this kitchen,” she tells the dough. “They’re going to find me in the bread.”
