s12.slug: THURSDAY · 6:40 PM · THE FRONT ROOM — LA VIGILIA
body: The dining table has been carried into the front room, where there’s space for it, with the card table butted onto the end under the same white cloth, and Nonna is at the head in her own chair with the tree lit behind her. At twenty to seven Ma comes in from the kitchen with the bread and sees what Nonna has done.

Nonna set it while Ma was down in the basement: at her right hand, where it has always been, a plate, a glass, and the napkin ring from his First Communion, silver plate gone soft at the edges, *D.F.C. 1995*, with one of the good napkins drawn through it.

Ma stops with the bread. Down at the other end of the table Frank has seen it too, and the two of them look at each other the length of the cloth, and Ma puts the bread down beside it and goes back for the clams.

Theo, coming in behind her with the baccalà, sees it too. He sets the baccalà down, and goes out to the garage, and comes back with a folding chair with a union sticker on the back, and opens it at the corner by Rosie.

“Phones,” Ma says, and holds out the bread basket — the second one, the empty one, lined with a dish towel — at the end of the sideboard. Gina drops hers in with a sigh that goes on past the phone. Theo lays his iPhone in on top of it gently, a coat left at a coat check. Jack puts the RAZR in last, shut, and Ma sets the basket on the sideboard by the window and turns her back on it.
When Nonna is in and settled, Theo half rises off the folding chair. “I’m the guest —”
“You’re not company,” Frank says. “Rosie says it.”
Theo sits back down.

Rosie stands up on her chair rung to be taller and folds her hands under her chin and does the regular grace first, all of it, fast, as they say it at school, and then keeps going. Thank you for the fish, even the eel. And for Jack being home from California, and for Theo coming from California too. And for the baby in New Orleans. And for Danny, and that he gets to have Christmas where he is. And Nonna’s hand, that it gets better. And Theo’s mom, who has a coach. And the Browns. And Denver, her buffalo, who is under the tree and can’t come to the table. “And the baby in New Orleans,” she says, “again, because she’s new. Through Christ our Lord.”
“Amen,” says the table, and Theo a syllable behind it.

Ma is crying. She does every year at about this point, and Frank passes his handkerchief up the table to her hand over hand, the same as every year. By the amen the clams have gone cold in their shells.

The fish come around one after another. The smelts, fried crisp enough to eat heads and all; Rosie eats only the tails. The baccalà in its tomatoes; Nonna tastes it and sends a word down the table, and Ma says, “I know, Ma. I know.” The white fish, which Gina says is whiting and Frank says is whatever was on sale. The squid, fried, which Theo tells Nonna he personally interrogated. Theo eats everything. When the linguine comes he reaches for the grated cheese, and Nonna says “*No!*” from the head of the table loud enough to stop Rosie chewing.
“No cheese on fish,” Gina says. “She says in Calabria they’d run you out of town.”
“I withdraw the cheese,” Theo says, and puts it down very carefully, and Nonna looks at him with real affection for the first time since the squid.

The eel has been on the table since grace, fried in rounds in its Pyrex near Frank’s elbow — Nonna had it brought out first, so the men couldn’t hide behind anything — and through the smelts and the baccalà it hasn’t been touched. Frank has moved his water glass to the far side of his plate to be farther from it. At the linguine Nonna runs out of patience. She puts a round on Jack’s plate with her left hand, and one on Theo’s.
Frank takes out his wallet and lays a five on the cloth beside the baccalà.
“First one of you eats that,” he says. “Twenty-four years I never paid out.”

response: He eats it in two bites without letting himself think about it. It’s rich, oily, sweet under the crisp, and it tastes like a river. Frank looks at him over the baccalà, and pushes the five across it with one finger. “Your brother never would.”
Theo eats his after, slowly, with his eyes shut, explaining it to the table as he goes. There’s no money in it for him. Nonna pats the cloth beside her plate for both of them.

choices.text: “Theo’ll eat mine. He’s from Los Angeles; he eats anything with a story.”
response: Theo eats his own, and then Jack’s, and gives a speech in between about courage and the Romans and an eel he once declined in Kyoto, and at the end of it he asks Nonna, through Gina, for the story.

Nonna gives him one. The eel is the snake from the garden. On Christmas Eve you eat him, so he can’t make trouble in the new year. He swam to Calabria to get away, and her own mother caught him in the river with her hands, in 1931 — “She’s making this up,” Gina says. “*Zitta*,” says Nonna. Frank pays Theo the five.

He forks his round onto Nonna’s plate. She eats it with great satisfaction, in two bites, and says something about Calabria that makes Ma put her napkin over her mouth. “Translate,” Theo says. “No,” says Gina.
Theo eats his own with his eyes shut, explaining it to the table as he goes, and Frank pays him the five.

body: At two minutes to seven, with the linguine going around, the basket on the sideboard buzzes. The RAZR rattles against Theo’s iPhone under the dish towel like something trying to get out.
Rosie is nearest. She’s off her chair first: “*Jack!* Your phone!” — and has it out of the basket in her fist, shut, the little outer screen lit up blue —

And Theo is there before she can get it open. He’s out of the folding chair and has the RAZR out of her hand, shut, his palm over the little screen, without any hurry about it, the way you’d take the scissors from a kid who’s only holding them, and he passes it down the table to Jack face-down, without looking at it.
“Yours.”
Jack puts it in his pocket. His ears are hot.
“*Basket*,” Ma says.
He takes it back out and puts it in the basket. Theo is already back on the folding chair, asking Nonna for the bread. Gina has become very interested in a clam.

body: The linguine goes, and the shrimp, and the anchovy bread, the seventh. There are the honey cookies Ma and Gina fried Sunday night, and coffee. Frank undoes the top button of his good pants and announces it. The tree lights blink in the black of the front window.
At five to eight Jack is at the sideboard.
“Ma. The levee. I said I’d call.”
Ma looks at him from her end of the table with the coffee pot in her hand.
“Is that the girl?”
“It’s Lena.”
She holds the look one more second. “Take it,” she says. “Tell her Merry Christmas from the Costigans.”
He has the phone out of the basket, not dialed yet, when the table shouts it — *MERRY CHRISTMAS* — at it, Rosie loudest, Frank with his hands cupped.
From the head of the table Nonna lifts the beads: “*La suora!*”
“What’s a levee?” Rosie says.
“Where they light the fires,” Jack says, on his way.
“Tell her I ate an eel,” Theo says, loudly, to his back.
He goes out through the kitchen, past the pots soaking in the sink, and holds the side door so it won’t bang, and lets it close on the noise of all of them.
At eight o’clock he calls her from the garage.

His father’s garage at Christmas: the space heater ticking up to orange at his shins, the Stroh’s fridge humming to itself, the radio off tonight, and over the workbench the colored lights on the pegboard, one blue bulb dead in the middle, strung over the painted outlines of the tools. Jack has the Carhartt on over his good shirt, and squid on his hands that the sink didn’t get off.
“Don’t talk,” Lena says. “Listen.”

She holds the phone up. It comes down the line as a roar with cracks in it — the cane going off in the heat like cap guns, a string of firecrackers some cousin lit too close, kids shrieking, a man’s voice, *Remy, get back from that*, the deep soft rush of a big fire pulling air — and under all of it, thin and tinny out of a truck parked on the levee with its doors open, Louis Armstrong.

“That’s Lutcher,” she says when she brings it back. “Daddy’s arguing with a man from Gramercy about whose is bigger. Luc’s being a policeman about the firecrackers and nobody’s listening to him. Remy’s in the bed of the truck with a cousin I’ve never met who swears we’ve met. Wait, they’re —” and the phone’s up again, and the levee cheers something he can’t see.

He takes it out of the garage, down the driveway past his father’s truck. Christmas Eve has come in clear and bitter. The old snow on the lawns has frozen hard enough to stand on, Frank’s blue lights are on around the Madonna in the side yard, and in the south, over the roofs across Glenwood, there’s a half-moon, white and very sharp, cut clean down the middle. Through the front window the table is still out, and Theo is talking to Nonna with both hands, and Nonna is pretending not to understand him.
“Can you see the moon?” She has the phone back at her ear. The fire is behind her now, and her breath is close.
“I can see the moon.”

And the line goes quiet with both of them on it. The fire keeps on at her end, low. At his, the furnace kicks on in the house and a car goes by down at the corner with its radio up, and is gone. His breath goes up white toward the moon. There is room in it for anything either of them might say. He has a sentence; he holds it in his mouth like a coal. On her end she doesn’t fill it either: her breath, held a second and let go, and held again, as if she had one too. Then a firecracker goes off close to her, and some child screams with joy, and Lena laughs, and the quiet is over.
“I’m in Remy’s LSU sweatshirt and Mémère’s church gloves,” she says, “and I smell like a smokehouse.”
“I smell like squid.”
“Then we’d clear a room together.”
“How’s Nonna?”
“Worse. Better tonight. I told her about Mémère’s candle.” He tells her the rest: Nonna in her chair with the splint, sitting up for it. *Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.*
“*Tutto*,” Lena says. “Oh, I’m telling Mémère. She’ll light a second one out of competitiveness.”

He tells her Glenwood, since she told him the fire. The Madonna in her bathtub under the blue lights with snow on her shoulders — “A *bathtub* Mary? We have those. Mid-City’s full of them. Half the yards on Dupre.” “My grandfather dug ours in.” “So did half of Dupre.” Rosie’s grace, long enough that the clams went cold, with the baby in New Orleans in it. He leaves out the bread basket.
“She prayed for Lucille?”
“Twice, in case God missed it. ‘The baby in New Orleans.’ Then Theo, for coming.”
“Theo’s *there*?”
“In my father’s parka. He ate an eel. He wants you to know.”
“Lord. Tell him I’m proud of him. Tell him Papa Noël saw. And tell Rosie that Lucille says thank you — in those words. A godmother said so.”

body.text: “I ate mine first. Pop paid me five dollars across the baccalà.” “You took money off your father on Christmas Eve?” “It was a bet.” “It was a *sin*,” Lena says. “A small one. I’ll allow it.”
“He ate mine too. With a speech. He wanted the story.” “What’s the story?” “It’s an eel. There isn’t one. Nonna made one up for him.” “Then that’s the story,” Lena says.
“I gave mine to Nonna. She ate it in two bites and said something about Calabria Gina won’t translate.” “I like her more every time,” Lena says.

body: The baby stayed home with Tess and Beau and Mama; she is five days old and has a grip, Lena says, like a longshoreman. Then godmother: “I’ve been practicing my renunciations. I renounce Satan. I renounce all his works. I renounce the Dallas Cowboys.” She is telling him about her father when her father takes the phone.

“Is this the Ohio boy?” Tony Broussard, loud enough to carry over a fire. “Merry Christmas, son. Your Harrison ran for two hundred and eighty-six yards Sunday. I watched the highlights four times. I had money on Kansas City.”
“Merry Christmas, Mr. Broussard. I’m sorry about Kansas City.”
“You ought to be.” And, away from the phone: “He’s polite. Told you.” And the phone is hers again.
“He cried for ten minutes on a man from Metairie in the waiting room Saturday,” she says, “and found out afterward the man was a Falcons fan. They’re exchanging Christmas cards.”
“Julian lands the thirtieth,” she says. “Mémère’s ironing a tablecloth.”
There’s frost on the tailgate of his father’s truck, and when Jack takes his hand off it his palm has left a print there, melted down to the green paint.
“You stood up,” she says. “Didn’t you. In your kitchen.”
“With a squid in my hand.”

Her laugh goes up over the fire. Somebody near her asks what’s funny, and she says *the Pope*, and is told that isn’t funny, and laughs harder. Jack has his back against his father’s truck and the cold coming through the Carhartt, and doesn’t feel it.

“I had your holy card out on the counter for the rest of it,” she says. “Propped on the sugar. Facing the television, so he could watch himself get up.” A cheer goes up behind her. “They’re lighting the next one down. You can see four from here. Listen.”

On the levee a stack of cane goes up with a crack, and a cousin whoops at it. “You’d hate it,” Lena says, with a laugh that comes half a beat early. “Everybody’s cousin is here, and they all want to know about the Ohio boy.” The fire, and her breath. “Come stand on one sometime.”

body: At twenty-five to nine the cousins start loading the trucks at her end; he hears the tailgates. “Go back to your fishes, Youngstown,” Lena says. “I’ve got a Mass.”
“Midnight.”
“Ours is at midnight. Yours is at midnight.” A truck door, and her boots on gravel. “I’ll be an hour behind you all the way.”

Then neither of them says anything, again: the tailgates, the fire popping behind her, somebody calling her name off the levee, and her breath, close, not going anywhere. He doesn’t go anywhere either. “Okay,” she says, to nobody, or to him. She hangs up first.

He stays in the driveway a minute with the phone shut in his hand and his breath going up. The moon has moved west over the roofs. Somewhere toward Market Street a dog is barking at it, or at Christmas, and a door opens on a party two streets over and closes again.

In the garage the colored lights are on over the bench, and the space heater has the place nearly warm. He takes the tin out of the Carhartt and opens it on the workbench under the dead blue bulb — RELIQUARY in her marker on the lid, the corners gone shiny from a week in his pocket — and counts them with one finger, filter by filter. Eleven. He shuts the lid and puts it back in the pocket. The Marlboros ride in the other one.

Through the side door the kitchen is loud: Rosie still doing the donkey without the radio, the pans going into the sink, his mother calling his name, and Theo over all of it asking Nonna, in very bad Italian, whether there’s any more eel.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven.

s14.slug: FRIDAY · 12:00 AM · ST. BRIGID OF KILDARE, MIDNIGHT MASS
body: St. Brigid’s has every light on, the brass chandeliers lit end to end as they are twice a year, and by half past eleven the Christmas-and-Easter crowd is standing at the back under the choir loft in their good coats with the carols going over their heads. The poinsettias are banked three deep up the altar steps. The crèche is set up at the end of the communion rail on their side, the old plaster family under a roof of real straw, the manger still empty.

The Costigans have their pew, two-thirds of the way back on the left. Nonna is on the aisle with the splint in her lap, and Theo beside her in a tie she has retied twice since the house; then Rosie, Ma, Jack, Gina, and Frank on the end.

At midnight the bells go, and the procession comes up the middle in a cloud of incense, the servers and the candles and Father Dom at the back of it in gold, taking the altar steps one at a time on the bad knee with a server’s hand under his elbow. He lays the Child in the manger himself. The Gloria comes back after four Sundays without it, and Rosie, who has been waiting, sings it at the top of her lungs a half-beat ahead of the organ.

Mr. Yanko from the Knights reads Isaiah in his foreman’s voice, *The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light*, and Father Dom reads Luke. Frank goes to sleep on his feet somewhere around Quirinius, as he does every year, and at *Glory to God in the highest* Gina puts an elbow in him and he comes awake looking like he never left.
Father Dom keeps the homily to three sentences. “The angels didn’t go to the palace,” he says. “They went to the night shift. Every one of you knows somebody who works nights.” And he sits.
At the consecration the bells ring and the pew goes down onto the kneelers. Nonna’s hand comes over onto Theo’s shoulder to press him down, and finds him already going.

At the sign of peace the girl in the white knit hat two pews up turns around, and it’s Carly Benedetto, Mooney ’09, her mother beside her. “Peace be with you, Jack.” Her hand is cold. Her eyes go to his eyebrow and come back to his face.
“And also with you.”

Gina has her hand out for him, and Rosie leans across Ma to get him too, and the man behind them in the Steelers jacket wants him, so he gives the peace to all three. Over the side of the pew, in the crèche, the plaster ox has had a chipped horn since before Jack was born, and somebody has turned it again this year so the chip faces the wall.

body.text: When the pew goes up for Communion, Theo stays where he is, and so does Nonna; the aisle is too long for her tonight. Jack goes up with Ma and the girls and his father and receives in the hand, and coming back down the side aisle he sees one of the Altar and Rosary ladies stop at the end of their pew with the little gold pyx, and Nonna lift her face for it, and Theo beside her with his hands on his knees, sitting with her while it comes.

At the far end Theo stays where he is, and so does Nonna; the aisle is too long for her tonight. One of the Altar and Rosary ladies comes down to the end of the pew with the little gold pyx, and Nonna lifts her face for it, and Theo sits beside her with his hands on his knees while it comes. Jack kneels three people’s width from the two of them with his hands over his face and makes a spiritual communion, as the nuns taught them to for the nights you can’t.

body: They go out on “Joy to the World” with the doors open and the night coming in. Father Dom is at the back in the gold, shaking hands like anybody, a word for everyone. He takes Jack’s. “Merry Christmas, Jack.” There’s nothing in his face but the hour.
On the steps, in the crowd going down to the cars, Carly catches his sleeve. “You’re home.”
“Till the ninth.”
“There’s a thing at Ryan’s on New Year’s. YSU people.” Her mother is calling her from the curb. “Come.”
He nods, and she goes down to her mother.

Frank brings the truck around for Nonna and Ma, and Rosie is asleep across the bench seat before the doors are shut, so the other three walk: five blocks down the middle of Glenwood, because there isn’t a car moving on the South Side. The ground is frozen hard and the crust along the curbs creaks under them. Gina walks in the middle with an arm through each of theirs. Over the roofs the half-moon is going down, and at the corner of Brownlee Theo says, “In Los Angeles, Midnight Mass is at ten. So the valets can get home,” and Gina says, “The *valets*,” and says it again at the next corner, and hangs off the both of them the rest of the way up the street to the porch light.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall.

body: At twenty to six Danny’s bed is empty, the quilt turned back square. Out the window, in a gray rain coming down on the old snow, Theo is standing at the bathtub Madonna in the Browns parka with his bare hand on the rim of the tub, and Jack lets the blind go.

By six Nonna has the Pope on the little set at the end of the kitchen counter, up and unhurt on his balcony, blessing the city and the world. Rosie has been awake since a quarter to, sitting on the top stair in her nightgown with Denver the buffalo, because on Christmas morning nobody sets foot in the front room until Nonna is settled, and settling Nonna takes an hour. By ten after seven she is in her chair by the window with her coffee on the sill. Ma puts the Christmas disc in, the same one since Jack was in grade school, and The Band comes on low under the rain, and Rosie comes down the stairs like a fire drill.

There are eight stockings on the mantel this morning. The new one hangs on the end, past NONNA, and the glitter glue on its cuff hasn’t finished drying: THEO. Rosie delivers it to him with both arms. Theo sits on the couch with it across his knees and touches the H, and a little of the H comes off on his finger.
“It’s still wet.”
“I did it Monday night,” Ma says. “Glitter takes a week.”
There’s a tin of her cookies in it, and a tangerine in the toe. Theo keeps the stocking on his lap through everything after.

In Jack’s, under the tangerine, is a page of the phone bill, folded in thirds, the family plan with his line circled in ballpoint, and across the top in Ma’s school-office capitals: UNLIMITED TEXTING. MERRY CHRISTMAS. LOVE, MA. She called them Tuesday. “It was cheaper than you,” Ma says.
Gina sits straight up. “He gets *unlimited*?”
“When you go to California.”

After the stockings, the tree. Rosie delivers, every box, by herself. Theo’s presents come out of a Neiman Marcus bag one at a time. For Ma, an orange enamel pot from France that weighs more than Rosie, which Ma says is much too much and has the gravy started in while the paper is still on the rug. For Nonna, torrone “from the one shop in Beverly Hills a Calabrese would forgive”; Nonna reads the box at arm’s length and forgives it. For Gina, a Flip camera; she’s filming Theo with it with the plastic still on. For Rosie, a stuffed blue crab the size of a hubcap. “*Callinectes sapidus*,” Theo tells her. “The beautiful swimmer.” Rosie says it back to him twice, perfectly, and across the rug Gina looks at Jack. For Danny, by way of Jack, four used paperbacks with the prices still penciled inside the covers. “I *called*,” Theo says. “Softcover only. No staples. They have a list.”

For Frank, last, something flat in tissue. It’s a program: the 1964 championship game, Colts at Browns, Municipal Stadium, December 27th, foxed at the corners and soft with being kept. Frank holds it in both hands a long time.
“Sixty-four,” he says.

Jack has pictured this happening a lot of ways since Thanksgiving. None of them had the Dell on the kitchen table next to the butter dish.

body: It takes four minutes.

The fan page first: four thousand and change. “One of them is in *Brazil*.” Gina scrolls the Wall for them like the announcements at Mass: a girl in Tulsa who would die for Cassidy, a long one in Portuguese with a great many hearts in it. Then the network’s pictures, and three of Skye’s own, public, the kind anybody can see: Skye on a red carpet in a dress cut down to there in front; Skye in a bikini on somebody’s boat, at a dock off Catalina, squinting into the sun; Skye barefoot on the hood of the Saab with the top down, laughing at whoever has the camera.

Gina leaves the boat up. Rain ticks on the window over the sink, and Theo’s French pot has the gravy going on the back burner, and the Costigans and a Vance lean in around a fourteen-inch monitor on the kitchen table at a girl on a boat. In the picture her hair is wet and she has a can of Diet Coke in one hand and she’s laughing at somebody off the edge of the frame, and Jack knows that laugh; he has been the one off the edge of the frame. He keeps that off his face as well as he can. It isn’t very well.
The RAZR stays in Jack’s pocket, shut, with his hand on it.
“She’s in her underwear,” Ma says.
“It’s a *bathing suit*, Ma.”
“On a *boat*.”
Frank looks at the screen with his coffee halfway to his mouth, and doesn’t get it the rest of the way.
“Huh,” he says.
Nonna has her rosary out of her pocket. She says something low in Calabrese at the hood of the Saab, and then something lower.
“She says somebody get that girl a sweater,” Gina reports.
“And the other thing?”
“No.”
“Gina.”

“I will *never* say it.” Gina’s ears are red and she can’t keep her mouth straight. “Three seasons. She’s in every episode. The one who drowns in season two isn’t her. It’s really sad.” And low, to Jack, under the fan page: “I didn’t tell. I *gave you a present*.”
Rosie is kneeling up on a chair with her chin on the table and the blue crab under her arm. “She’s pretty.” She thinks about it. “Can I see the boat again?”
“No,” says Ma.
“There’s a promo,” Gina says. “For season three. She’s in a *pool*.”
“*No*,” says Ma.
Nonna lifts her chin off the beads and looks at Jack, very clear. “*E la suora?*”
Ma pulls her chair in closer to the table, and pushes it back out again. “What happened to the Saints girl?” she says. “She sent you a *book*.”
“The one he went out to the garage for,” Frank says.

Theo is at the counter with his coffee, in the hat and the scarf, the only one in the kitchen besides Jack who has ever met Skye Callender. “She’s very talented, Mrs. Costigan.” He drinks some coffee. “Lena called from a levee. It was on fire.”
“This one goes to school with you?” Ma says.
“Starting January.”
Ma, to the coffee: “Starting January.”

She gets up, and takes her cup to the sink, and runs the water with her back to all of them. Out the window over the sink the rain is coming down on the garage roof and the Madonna and the Kovacs’ fence, and the snow is going gray in the yard.
“Is she *Catholic*, at least?”

body: It rains all morning. It comes down on the porch roof in a long hush and off the gutters in strings, and the old snow in the yards has gone gray and is shrinking into the gutters as he watches. Jack has the tarp pulled back off the glider and Nonna’s afghan over his knees. At 9:40 the RAZR goes.
“Are you on the glider?” Skye says.
“Under the tarp.”

“Good. Stay there.” She’s on her mother’s balcony in Studio City; there’s traffic on a big road somewhere below her and, close to the phone, a bird clearing its throat. “That’s the parrot. It says *momager*. It says *Merry Christmas* now too — my mother taught it for the network party. Now. Who. How. Everything. In order. Don’t skip, I’ll know.”

So he gives it to her in order. Gina’s present, wrapped in the *Vindicator*’s funnies; Rosie handing it to him in front of everybody, Gina too late to stop her; the box set; the Post-it. The front window behind him is full of his family pretending to do something else: Gina at the glass with her arms crossed, Rosie with her nose on it, his mother behind them with the curtain in her hand, and Theo at the back, in the new Browns hat, reading the DVD box.
“And my grandmother points at the cover,” he says, “and says *L’attrice!*”
“She *pointed*?”
“At the girl in the middle. In the blazer.”
“That’s season two,” Skye says. “I was eighteen and they had me in a blazer with *shoulder pads*. Keep going.”

The Dell on its extension cord on the kitchen table. Gina, four minutes, her own account. The fan page — Brazil. The boat. Nonna with her rosary out, saying things in Calabrese that Gina wouldn’t translate. His father, who looked at the screen for a long time and then said: “Huh.”
“That’s a *rave*,” Skye says. “That’s four stars. I’m putting it on the poster. Wave at them.”
“No.”
“Wave at them, Jack.”
He turns around on the glider and waves at the window. Gina waves back. Rosie waves with both hands. His mother lets the curtain drop.
“What did your mother say? Don’t give me the gist. Give me the line.”

He tells her: Ma at the sink, with her back to the room and the water running. *Is she Catholic, at least?* He tries to tell her how it sounds — the flat Valley *a*’s, the *at least* coming down on the end of it like the lid on a pot.
Skye is quiet for about as long as it takes to try it in her mouth. And she does it. “*Is she Catholic, at least?*”
It’s near enough that he looks over his shoulder at the window.

“Jack.” She’s starting to go. “Jack. They know me as the *nice* one. I’m on a boat in a bikini on the kitchen table and your grandmother’s praying the rosary at me, and it says on the DVD that I’m the NICE one. They think I’m *Cassidy*.” And she’s gone: she’s put the phone down on the balcony rail to laugh, and he can hear her a little way off from it, helpless, and the parrot, much closer, says something into the mouthpiece in a language of its own. When she picks it up again she’s out of breath. “I’m having it put on my headstone. *Here lies the nice one.*”
The rain comes harder for a minute and lets up.
“Your mother didn’t ask if I’m Catholic,” Skye says. “She asked if you still are.”
“She asked if you were.”
“She asked it to the sink,” Skye says. “With the water running. I’ve played that mother. Twice. One time I was the daughter. Nobody asks a faucet a question they want answered.”
He doesn’t have anything ready for that. He looks at the street, the water running in the gutter toward Market, the Santa two doors up lying in a puddle now instead of a drift.
“I’d like to be in that kitchen,” she says. “Your grandmother would hate me. I’d win her by Easter.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone.

response: “They’re scared of you,” he says.

The parrot fills the gap. Then: “Good,” Skye says. “I’m scared of them.” And straight on from it she wants to know what Nonna said in Calabrese, exactly, and whether Gina translated, and he tells her Gina refused.

Behind her the parrot says *Merry Christmas* in her mother’s network voice, and somebody inside calls her name. “That’s my mother. There’s a hotel, and a brunch, and the omelet man is expecting me.” She stops at the door; the slider rumbles in its track. “Merry Christmas, Ohio. Tell Ted the girl he was careful with says hi.”

She’s gone. The rain comes off the end of the gutter in a rope and spatters the steps. body: At a quarter past two the phone rings on the kitchen wall by the pantry, its long cord hanging down in loops to the linoleum, and on the second ring Ma is there, a dish towel in her other hand. The little set at the end of the counter has the news on low. A woman’s recorded voice comes out of the receiver loud enough for the table: *This is a collect call from* — and Danny, fast, saying his own name into the space they give him — *an inmate at an Ohio correctional institution. This call may be monitored and recorded.* Ma presses the button while the woman is still talking.
“Merry Christmas, baby.”

She takes him into the pantry with the cord pinched under the door and is in there a minute with the canned tomatoes. When she comes out she holds the receiver down to Nonna’s chair in the doorway, and Nonna takes it in her left hand and listens with her eyes shut.
“Danny.” Then: “*Viene?*”
Ma takes it back from her gently and hands it on to Frank, who stands with the receiver against his ear and his other hand in his pocket and gives his son two sentences.
“Harrison ran two-eighty-six. Here’s your sister.”

Gina has been waiting. She takes the phone into the corner by the refrigerator, as far as the cord goes, and turns her back on the kitchen. It doesn’t help. “Danny. *Danny.* You don’t even know. She was on a *boat*. A boat with a *bathroom* on it. And then she’s barefoot on a *car* —”
“On a boat,” Ma says, at the stove.
“A *different* picture, Ma. Danny, there’s a fan page. Somebody in *Brazil* —” And out of the receiver, from across the kitchen, small and clear and helpless, comes Danny’s laugh.

Rosie gets the phone next, for about ten seconds, and spends them on the crab: it’s blue, it has a Latin name, the Latin name means *beautiful swimmer*, Theo said, Theo is here, Theo ate an eel. Danny is still laughing when Rosie hands the phone to Jack. Danny tries twice to say something and can’t get through it. The third time he makes it.
“You said she does *plays*.”
Gina wheels around by the refrigerator. “He *told* you?”
“He told me she *reads*, G,” Danny says, loud enough to carry, and keeps the rest. At the stove, with the wooden spoon stopped in the gravy, Ma looks at Jack, and then goes back to stirring.
“What’d you tell her, Professor?” Danny says. “You’re a doctor?”
“I told her about you.”
“Then she’s got guts,” Danny says. “Put the rich one on.”
Theo takes the phone in the orange hat. Danny’s voice comes out of it, tinny. “Two days running, man. Ma’s gonna claim you on her taxes.”
“She glued my name on a stocking.”
“Then that’s it.” Behind him, a room full of men and somebody’s name on a loudspeaker. “You’re on the list out there too. You don’t get off that one.”
Theo looks at the receiver in his hand. Then he gives it back to Jack fast, cord and all, and goes to see about the Tupperware.
There’s a tone on the line: a minute left. Danny comes back on lower, close to the mouthpiece, so whatever he means by it stays on Jack’s end.
“Tell the TV girl I said she can do better than you. And tell the veil girl —”
A click, and the dial tone.

Jack stands by the pantry with it humming in his ear. Gina is still holding her hand out for another turn. Nobody in the kitchen says anything, and after a minute Ma takes the receiver out of his hand and hangs it up on the wall.

At half past three the news on the little set changes its voice. A Northwest flight from Amsterdam, coming down into Detroit before noon: a passenger, something he had in his lap, a pop and then a fire, and the people around him on top of him before it could catch. They don’t have a name yet. They show a plane parked by itself, far out on the concrete.
“On *Christmas*,” Frank says.
Ma turns around from the stove. “You’re flying *tonight*?”
“They’ll be very thorough,” Theo says.

At half past four he comes down the stairs in the camel coat with the garment bag over his shoulder, in the Browns hat and the Browns scarf, without the parka. Jack carried his other bag down for him and saw it on the way, folded square at the foot of Danny’s bed. Ma has a Giant Eagle bag of Tupperware waiting by the side door, every lid labeled in her capitals: BACCALÀ. COOKIES. MORE COOKIES. FOR YOUR MOTHER. Gina films all of it on the Flip.

Nonna is in her chair in the front window with the cashmere over her knees and her hand on it. Theo bends down to her. She says something to him in Calabrese that Gina doesn’t translate, and pats his face, and he tucks the cashmere in along her side where it has come loose, and straightens up, and leaves it there.

body.text: At the side door he stops with his hand on the frame, and says it lower, under the noise of Ma looking for a bigger bag. “Be careful, Costigan.” “Of what?” “*All* of it.”

body: “Come back on the ninth,” Theo says, out on the step, with the rain coming off the gutter behind him. “Laney has a *schedule*.”
Jack laughs. “Of course she does.”

Frank has the Silverado running in the driveway with the wipers going. He leans across and shoves the passenger door open, and says it through the rain while Theo is still on the step: “You come back.”
“I’ll call first, sir.”
“Don’t,” Frank says, and Theo gets in.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Three in the morning on Christmas, in Danny’s bed, I told him she’d told me. He wasn’t surprised.

journal.title: Ma
journal.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.”

s18.slug: FRIDAY · 9:05 PM · THE SILVERADO, IN THE DRIVEWAY
body: It has rained all of Christmas, and at nine it’s still coming, steady and gray through the streetlight, running down the windshield of his father’s truck in sheets. Jack sits behind the wheel in the driveway with the engine going for the heater and the wipers off, and the house beside him is lit in every window: the tree in the front one, Nonna’s lamp, his mother crossing the kitchen. The rain drums on the cab roof a foot over his head.

Lena is on the back steps on Dupre Street with the screen door behind her. Christmas dinner is over and the house isn’t; every time the door opens he gets it — voices, a television, dishes — and then the spring pulls it to. Remy is singing in the kitchen, badly, on purpose. Tess has the baby asleep on her in the front room, Lena says, and nobody is allowed to breathe in that direction. Lucille slept through her first Réveillon and woke up for the café brûlot. Daddy is calling it a sign.
“Tell me yours first,” she says. “Start at the stairs.”

He starts at the stairs. Rosie on them at six, made to wait till Nonna was settled. His mother’s Christmas CD, the same one since he was in grade school. Theo’s present to his father: a program from the 1964 championship game, and his father holding it in both hands a long time and saying *Sixty-four*.
“Browns?”
“Twenty-seven, nothing, over the Colts. The last thing they ever won.”
“Theo found that?”
“Theo found that. He gave Rosie a stuffed blue crab and taught her the Latin.”
“*Callinectes sapidus*,” Lena says. “Daddy sells them by the bushel. Tell Rosie hers is the best one north of Memphis.” The baby, very faintly, through two walls. “Is he still there?”
“Pop drove him to Pittsburgh at four-thirty.”
“With that man on the news?”
“He says they’ll be very thorough.”
“Make him text you when he lands.” And then: “What else?”
“Ma brewed your coffee.”
“And?”
“It’s gone. The can’s empty.”
“Good.”
“She asked where I got New Orleans coffee.”
“And what’d you tell her?”
“A friend.”
In the kitchen on Dupre Street Remy reaches for a note that isn’t there. “Well,” Lena says. “That’s true.”
“Father Dom preached three sentences at midnight,” he says. “The angels didn’t go to the palace. They went to the night shift.”
“Luc’s on nights all week.” Somebody goes past her into the house with a stack of plates. “I’m telling him a priest in Ohio said so.”
“What’d Papa Noël bring Dupre Street?”

“Daddy got everybody the same thing. Brees jerseys. All of us, the baby included — hers goes to her knees. Mémère wore hers to dinner over her church dress, and Mama took a picture, and it’s going on next year’s card whether Mémère likes it or not.”

“Julian called at dinner,” she says. “From Oakland. His brother’s ship is in for Christmas, so the whole Park-Ellis side was on the line yelling *Merry Christmas* at the whole Broussard side.” A breath. “He asked to say hi to Lucille. He sang her ‘You Are My Sunshine,’ all the way through, every verse, even the sad one nobody knows, over the speakerphone at the table. Tess cried. Daddy said it was the onions.” Somebody laughs behind the screen door. “He’s good with babies. I didn’t know that.”
The wipers are off. The rain sheets down the glass.
“That’s nice of him,” he says.

body.text: “I said I’d tell you about ours,” she says, straight on, with no room left in between.
She goes straight on, with no room left in between.

body: “You already know the menu.”
“Tell me anyway.”
He turns the heater fan down a notch to hear her better, and slides down in the seat until his head is against the back window of the cab, and shuts his eyes.

So she tells him Réveillon the way it went, dish by dish. The grillades and grits went first, as always. The daube didn’t set. Mama made it Tuesday and it sat in the icebox two days refusing to be anything but soup, and at two in the morning Daddy declared it a new dish and named it for Luc, and everybody ate it with a spoon. Mémère and Mama fought over the roux for forty minutes in two languages, and Mémère won, and Mama says she let her. Remy put too much whiskey in the sauce for the bread pudding, on purpose. Josie was asleep under the table by three with her head on Jude’s shoes. And Daddy did the café brûlot in the good bowl, by the curtains, with the lights out, while Mama told him not by the curtains, and the curtains are fine — Mama has said *the curtains are fine* four times today, and every time it sounds less true.
With his eyes shut Dupre Street is in the truck with him — the curtains, the spoon in the soup that was supposed to be daube, Josie under the table — and he lets her finish.

“Mémère gave the toast,” she says. “In French, the same one every year. This year she put Lucille in it. Then she put Grandmère in it. Then she sat down.” On her end a car goes by on Dupre Street, slow, in the wet. “And Mama set Grandmère’s place. Like every year. The plate, and the glass, and the good napkin.” Behind her the screen door opens on somebody laughing and closes on it. “Tess came in from the car with the baby in the carrier, and she set it on the chair to get her coat off. Just for a minute. That chair. And Mama picked it up and put it on the floor, and didn’t say a word. And then she picked it back up and put it back on the chair. And then nobody said anything till the gumbo.”
The rain on the roof. The heater, still catching up.
“My mama worked at Memorial,” Lena says.
The rain comes down the windshield in the dark, and the porch light two houses up runs to pieces in it.

response: He sits up, and stays on the line. The rain on the roof. On her end the screen door, a dish breaking somewhere in the house and a cheer going up for it, the baby starting in the front room and Tess walking her quiet again. Her breath against the phone, and his, and the wipers off, and the windshield running.
“Thank you,” she says. And a minute later, lower: “I’ve never said that out loud on purpose.”

response: “Do you want to tell me?”
“No,” she says. “Not tonight.” The screen door; Remy getting louder in the kitchen and somebody telling him to hush; the baby. “Someday, maybe.”

response: “Nonna set a place for Danny last night,” Jack says. “His plate. His glass. Ma left it there.”
The rain. Her breath on the line. “Then we both had one,” Lena says.

response: “Danny called today,” Jack says. “From Trumbull. The phone cut him off right when he got to you.”
A breath on her end, a long one. “Tell him I heard it anyway.”

response: “What happened there?”

It’s the arguer’s question, and it’s out, and on the steps she goes quiet. The screen door. The house. “Not tonight, Jack,” she says, gently, and closes it. She tells him about Josie’s agenda for the baptism instead — typed, with a section for Josie’s own remarks — and he lets her, and laughs where he’s supposed to.

s18a.slug: FRIDAY · 9:50 PM · THE SILVERADO, IN THE DRIVEWAY
body: By ten to ten they’ve gotten around to the book.

“Forty pages,” Jack says. It’s on the dash. He knows the book; he didn’t know it with her in the margins, small and fast and merciless, a *ha* here and a *no* there, and *oh, honey* beside Binx on the Gentilly bus. “Binx is a lot.”
“Binx Bolling is every man who ever lived,” Lena says. “That’s the *point*.”
“You wrote that it’s Carnival in there.”
“It is. Kate, the parades, the week before Ash Wednesday. You’re reading Carnival.”
“It’s raining in Youngstown.”
“Then it’s Carnival in the rain,” Lena says. “That still counts. Ask anybody on St. Charles.”
“I’ll ask Binx.”
“Binx would say it doesn’t count,” she says, “and then go anyway. Sunday’s Tampa. You’re watching. I don’t care if it’s the radio in the garage.”
“It’s the radio in the garage.”
“Then the radio.”

body.text: “Mama says the mailman left a slip on Christmas Eve,” she says. “Something from Ohio. I’m not allowed to guess. I’ll tell you what I think when it’s open.”

body: On her end the screen door opens and somebody says her name, and she says *one minute* in a voice that means five. “Lucille’s awake,” she says. “I’m on duty.”

body.text: “Merry Christmas, Youngstown,” she says.

body: “Merry Christmas, Lena.”
Neither of them hangs up. On Dupre Street the screen door opens again and somebody says her name again, nearer.
“Go,” he says. “You’re on duty.”
“I’m going.” She doesn’t, for a breath. Then the line is only the rain.
He sits with the phone in his lap. The heater has caught up at last, warm on his shins, and the rain goes on coming down the glass.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else.

body: The tree is the only light on in the front room. Ma left the Christmas disc going for Nonna when she went up, low, and it has come around by now to the last track. The rain has eased to a drip off the porch roof, and the street outside is black and wet to the end of the block. The house is asleep over his head. Gina’s light went off under her door at eleven. Upstairs, the parka is still folded on Danny’s bed, and Danny’s bed is made. On the mantel the eighth hook is empty; Theo took the stocking with him, glitter and all.

Nonna is awake in her chair by the window with the rosary moving in her good hand, a bead at a time, slower than the song. On the coffee table, under the markers in their open tin, is the drawing Rosie made after supper and left out for him: a girl in a navy blazer with yellow hair, and Jack beside her, very tall, and at their feet, bigger than either of them, a blue crab.
Jack sits down on the end of the couch in his socks, with the rain from the driveway still in his hair. He has had the phone in his hand since the truck. At two minutes to midnight it goes.

body.text: merry christmas from a hotel. my mother got a suite so nobody would have to cook. room service has a tree. its very small and very sad and i love it
cassidy says goodnight to your grandmother

body: He reads it in the dark with the phone close to his face. He can picture it: a hotel suite in Los Angeles, a tree no bigger than a lamp on the room-service cart, Skye in a hotel robe cross-legged on a bed the size of the Costigans’ kitchen, watching the clock on the cable box come around to nine. He can hear her doing Cassidy’s voice for the tree.

When he looks up, Nonna is watching him. She isn’t looking at his face. She’s looking at the phone, lit in his hand, with her head a little on one side, the way she looks at a pot she wasn’t told about.
“*Due ragazze*,” she says.
Then her eyes come up to his, and she is entirely here.
“*Quale ti fa pregare?*”
He knows every word of it.

He doesn’t answer her. After a while Nonna looks down again, and moves a bead along, and her lips start up where they left off. On the disc the song comes to its end, low, and stops. The tree lights stand in the wet window. Nonna’s beads click, and click again.

journal.title: Nonna
journal.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees.

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab.
